item.title: Thoughts on Yumi and the Nightmare Painter
item.description: For those unfamiliar, Brandon Sanderson is an eminent fantasy writer known for great worldbuilding and creative magic systems.
item.content:encoded:
For those unfamiliar, Brandon Sanderson is an eminent fantasy writer known for great worldbuilding and creative magic systems. Despite numerous recommendations of his work and attempts to get into his work, it just wasn’t for me. I’m not a big fantasy guy because I don’t care much for worldbuilding. And when I do enjoy a fantasy story, it’s because of strong character writing—not the fantasy elements themselves. However, I am a big fan of romance anime and manga. Give me two well-written characters with good chemistry, no unnecessary drama, and a generous sprinkle of wholesomeness and I’m sold. So when I saw that Brandon Sanderson had written a romance novel inspired by Makoto Shinkai’s Your Name, I thought it was the perfect opportunity to finally get into Sanderson’s work.

I’m proud to say that I recently finished Yumi and the Nightmare Painter. This isn’t a review or an analysis. These are my unfiltered thoughts about a romance so beautiful I can’t not write about it. This will contain major spoilers for the novel, which I highly recommend you read.

I wasn’t invested in Yumi and the Nightmare Painter (YNP) until the first chapter where Yumi and Nikaro met. The two characters are interesting enough on their own, but their chemistry is easily my favorite part of the story. Unfortunately, the novel focused far more on its fantasy elements than I would’ve liked. I acknowledge that I’m not Sanderson’s target audience of fantasy enthusiasts. That said, despite how well executed the worldbuilding and plot twists were, every time the story focused on the core conflict I felt like I was ravenously waiting for the next morsel of romance. When reminiscing about the story, I think not of the fact that Yumi and Nikaro’s worlds are the same, the twist that Yumi’s entire world is an illusion, that the nightmares are man-made, or even that Yumi lived through a time-loop; I think of those small moments of joy they shared: their baths, the carnival, and their final kiss.

I’m conflicted. On one hand, Yumi and Nikaro are easily one of my favorite couples in fiction. On the other, I wanted far more romance both interspersed throughout the plot and at the end of the story. Honestly, a spinoff slice-of-life sequel novel would be a dream come true. I’m so offended by the lack of similar YNP fanfiction that I’m tempted to write one myself and petition Brandon Sanderson to write a sequel (or at least a short story).

Before I gush about Yumi and Nikaro’s romance I want to briefly comment on a secondary idea of YNP: art is a functionless yet valuable and necessarily human creation. The story seems to use the scholar’s machine as an allegory for AI art generators. Like the machine, AI sacrifices the quality of human art for convenience. Unfortunately, beyond this, the allegory falls apart. First, the machine is a substitute for the strenuous, unpleasant labor of the yoki-hijo. Yumi isn’t happy dedicating her entire life to communing with the spirits via stacking. In contrast, most artists cherish their work. Second, stacking, unlike real-world art, is vital to basic societal functioning. The spirit machines, under proper function, would have proliferated Torio’s basic infrastructure and reduced dependence on scarce yoki-hijos (I reiterate, this is only if the machines functioned properly). The crucial distinction between stacks and art is that more stacks—regardless of quality—are theoretically beneficial. The same cannot be said of art. I’m not a big fan of this allegory, though I’d love to know if I’m missing something.

Where do I even begin with Yumi and Nikaro’s romance? Sanderson characterized them so that I desperately wanted each of them to be happy: Yumi free of her obligations and Nikaro vindicated of his wrongdoings. Then he organically pushed them together in a way that perfectly allowed them to grow. Nikaro’s free-spiritedness encouraged Yumi to develop agency and Yumi’s reverence for duty convinced Nikaro he was a good person. He even wrote a shared similarity between them: their ability to persistently do the right thing no matter how others treated them. That wizard Sanderson wrote excellent banter. Yumi’s uptightness and Nikaro’s flippant attitude play off of each other exquisitely. I was afraid Nikaro’s former crush on Akane would devolve into a needless love triangle (I was relieved by the lack of unnecessary romantic drama in the story). No unnecessary drama. No doubt that the two truly loved each other or should belong together. The cherry on top was that Yumi and Nikaro enjoyed an unambiguously happy ending.

I can’t remember the last time I cared so much for a fictional couple. Despite the drudgery I felt in the fantasy elements of the novel, it’s the little romantic moments that make YNP, in my eyes, the kind of thing that makes life just that little bit more meaningful.

I plead the universe that Sanderson or some enthusiastic fan writes more about these two. Please.

item.title: On Romance Tropes
item.description: I’m a big fan of romance in stories, whether it be minor subplots in video games, couples in battle shonen, or bona fide romance anime.
item.content:encoded:
I’m a big fan of romance in stories, whether it be minor subplots in video games, couples in battle shonen, or bona fide romance anime. I remember loathing romance when I was in elementary school because I viewed it as “lame” compared to literally any other part of a story.

Something about romance clicked for me in 6th grade when I read the first volume of Bakuman by Takeshi Obata and Tsugumi Ohba. Bakuman is a manga about two middle school students who become professional manga artists. It’s well regarded in the animanga community for its realistic portrayal of the manga industry and enjoyable characters. What captivated my middle school self, however, was its romance subplot. The melodramatic infatuation the protagonist felt towards his crush, the uncertainty of whether she reciprocated his feelings, and the relatable school setting made my heart pound. I realized how exhilarating romance could be.

I never finished Bakuman; the story became repetitive to me and I no longer care for its romance subplot. In 8th grade, I descended the romance animanga rabbit hole beginning with Toradora! and Teasing Master Takagi-san. I devoured the smorgasbord of romance tropes to the point where I knew what I loved.

I enjoy romance primarily because it makes me feel happy. I love seeing two likeable, well-written characters develop through their chemistry with each other. I like the wholesomeness, the emotional intensity, and the intimacy. A good romance lets you see people at their strongest and their most vulnerable, their best and their worst, their happiest and their saddest. The broader appeal of romance, however, lies in its potential for escapism. Fictional storytelling in general is an effective method of escapism. Add to that the near-universal relatability1 and euphoria of romantic love and it becomes evident why the fictional romance landscape is so riddled with clichés. The ubiquitous lack of quality in romance stories can be summed up as this: people love to insert themselves into characters living a wish-fulfillment fantasy.

Unfortunately, this often directly conflicts with why I enjoy romance. Wish-fulfillment narratives typically feature protagonists with no defining traits, which then precludes the emergence of a strong couple character dynamic. Tropes emerge in specific cultural contexts in ways that are over simplistic, unrealistic, or repetitive. Below I discuss romantic tropes that I like and dislike2:

Tropes I Dislike:

  1. The Self-insert Protagonist: Self-insert protagonists are obnoxious enough. They’re especially obnoxious in the romance genre because of how they’re depicted as ‘quirky’ or ‘misunderstood’. A textbook example of this is the stereotypical Webtoon romance protagonist, a seemingly ordinary girl who actually isn’t like the other girls and is fully deserving of the attention of numerous debonair suitors.

  2. ‘Perfect’ Love Interests: These love interests, commonly paired with self-insert protagonists, pander to the sensibilities of the target demographic. They are essentially ‘perfect’ people and often deserve a far better partner than the protagonist. Authors often attempt to showcase ‘flaws’ in them, which are actually portrayed as attractive or brushed aside. Rarely are the flaws of these characters portrayed as truly unattractive or problematic. One could argue that real people are attractive because of their flaws. The difference is that the flaws of real people pose less obscured issues.

  3. Actually Toxic Relationship: When the protagonist pursues a blatantly toxic or problematic relationship. I’m all for flawed characters bettering each other through romance. My problem is with problematic relationships being portrayed as healthy. An example of this is a young woman serving as a secretary to a (usually much older) CEO who enters a relationship with her. Another example is when a character repeatedly sexually harasses another character, only to end up with them later. What’s interesting about these tropes is that they reveal insidious cultural conceptions of our society. Using the above examples, that 1) exploitative power dynamic relationships persist, and 2) harassment is treated as permissible when the characters are attractive or eventually receptive towards it.

  4. Unnecessary Relationship Drama: When characters break up, date, or cheat for reasons out of character. I’ve noticed that American TV shows in particular refuse for their characters to maintain happy, healthy relationships. One explanation is that tumultuous romantic history—rife with adultery, breakups, and dating around—-is realistic. I find this explanation kind of depressing. Another explanation is that relationship drama is an easy way of repeatedly producing conflict in the plot, especially in shows that are dragged out. This explanation is also depressing. I gravitate more towards romance where two characters maintain a wholesome relationship with minimal friction across a story. This is admittedly less common. Perhaps the solution is not to calibrate the extent of romantic idealism in stories, but to ensure that drama emerges organically.

  5. Love Triangles: This ties into my feelings about unnecessary relationship drama. Love triangles can be executed well, but often produce tension I find unpleasant. They also encourage authors to artificially create romantic chemistry between multiple characters instead of focusing on a single couple.

  6. Harems: Same issue that I have with love triangles. The tension of who the protagonist will choose in a harem is unpleasant to me. Harems similarly encourage authors to artificially create romantic chemistry between multiple characters instead of focusing on a single couple.

  7. End of Story Confession: When two characters who have had strong romantic chemistry for much of the story only end up together at the end. This is much less forgivable in the romance genre. While I like a good slow burn romance with buildup to when the characters start dating, romantic character dynamics are far more enjoyable when the characters are actually dating.

My distaste for these tropes is so strong that I rarely deign to consume romance media featuring them. Any romance connoisseurs reading this might observe that I’ve just excluded virtually all mainstream portrayals of romance. Lucky me.

Tropes I Like:

  1. Keep It Simple: I don’t know if it’s even right to call this a trope so much as a set of conditions. A Keep It Simple (KIS) romance is one where: 1) Two characters fall in love early on in the story. 2) They spend a substantial portion of the story dating. 3) They end up together with little to no uncertainty. 4) There is no breakup, love triangle, adultery, on-and-off relationship, or will they won’t they nonsense. Minimal lies, conflict, and misunderstanding. This fourth condition is by far the most important to me. A KIS couple is to me the holy grail of fictional romance. It’s the difference between eating a meal prepared by a five star chef regularly and being malnourished, subsisting only on occasional acrid slop.

  2. Happy Epilogue: An epilogue or denouement to the story where the couple is seen happily thriving. It could be a wedding or even a scene of a couple now having kids. These scenes are the cherry on a top of a romance—the blissful reassurance that two characters lived happily ever after.

  3. Tsundere: Contrary to popular belief, a tsundere is not a girl in anime who violently abuses her crush. It’s a character who appears cold on the outside, yet is kind and warm on the inside. Something about people whose kindness belies their exterior really resonates with me. To me, the appeal of romance involving tsundere characters is that they are deeply misunderstood. This leads to a gradual reveal of their true nature and subsequent catharsis in seeing them reveal their inner affection to someone who truly cherishes them.

I could probably wax on endlessly about more specific tropes3 I like or dislike in romance, but I think I’ve conveyed my point. The deluge of romance tropes infesting fiction can make me forget how much joy fictional romance brings me at its best. It’s a testament to happiness storytelling imparts.

Thanks for reading my Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

I wonder how aromantic/asexual people feel about romance in media. Maybe it’s dreadful to some and like a zoo of foreign behavior to others.

2

You’ll notice that the tropes I like are directly related to the fundamental reasons I love romance. Similarly, the tropes I dislike are directly related to the issues that stem from wish-fulfillment fantasies. Also, forgive the listicle format.

3

I’m considering writing a comprehensive list of my relationship with various fictional tropes, or at least the ones most important to me. Is this worthwhile?

item.title: Personality Probabilistic Model (PPM)
item.description: A mental model for conceptualizing the relationship between personality traits and outcomes
item.content:encoded:
This is a prototypical, amateurish mental model of personality traits. I assume a rudimentary knowledge of probability distributions, expected value, and discrete/continuous random variables. Note that I am not an expert in personality psychology and simply sought to verbalize intuitions lingering in my head.

Imagine personality traits as existing on a spectrum. It could be one of the Big Five personality traits, an MBTI trait, etc. I make the following assumptions about these traits:

  1. Neutral point: Each spectrum has a ‘neutral’ point. This point represents the mean, median, default, or neutral expression of some personality trait.

  2. Infinite range: I assume that sometimes there is no theoretical limit to the magnitude of a personality trait. Some traits, however, have arguably finite levels of expression.

  3. Ordinal Quantifiability: Each individual has some “true” value on each personality spectrum. For example, everyone has a true level of extraversion. We seek to quantify personality in relative terms. That is, the scale of the spectrum doesn’t matter.

  4. Continuity: Some personality traits are continuous-valued, while others are discrete-valued.

I consider these three fairly reasonable assumptions. Here are some examples of traits modeled with these assumptions:

  • Extraversion: The neutral point is perfect ambiversion. The spectrum extends infinitely to the left (representing level of introversion) and to the right of the neutral point (representing level of extroversion). Extraversion is continuous-valued.

  • Psychopathy: The neutral point is zero psychopathy. The spectrum extends finitely in one direction, representing the level of psychopathy. Someone on the end of the spectrum is a full-blown psychopath. Those further on the spectrum are more psychopathic than those closer to the neutral point. Psychopathy is continuous-valued.

  • Empathy: The neutral point is complete indifference towards others. The spectrum extends infinitely to the left (representing level of antipathy) and to the right (representing level of empathy). Empathy is continuous-valued.

  • IQ: The neutral point is the median IQ of 100. The spectrum extends infinitely to the left (representing increasingly low IQ) and the right (representing increasingly high IQ). IQ is an ordinal measure. It’s quantified as an integer, so it’s discrete (not continuous).

These spectra are each called a personality spectrum. Each personality spectrum corresponds to a personality distribution, a probability distribution of personality traits on the spectrum. IQ, for instance, is normally distributed.

Now we select some arbitrary outcome variable, a quantifiable measure of performance in a scenario. An example of an outcome variable is SAT score. Given a personality spectrum, every locus of the spectrum corresponds to an outcome distribution, a probability distribution of the outcome variable. The expected value of the outcome distribution is the expected outcome. Suppose, using IQ as a personality spectrum, we select an IQ of 140. With SAT score1 as our outcome variable, the outcome distribution might look like this:

The expected outcome (the expected value of this outcome distribution) is 1430. That is, on average, someone with an IQ of 140 would score 1430 on the SAT. According to the empirical rule, an individual of 140 IQ is ~95% likely to score a 1370–1490. Instead of a locus, we can select a region of the personality spectrum. Suppose we select IQ ranging from 140–1602, with SAT score as our outcome variable. The outcome distribution of this region of the personality spectrum might look like this:

This outcome distribution is the aggregate of outcome distributions of all IQ values ranging from 140–160 averaged together3. For those curious, the expected outcome of this outcome distribution is ~1560.

To recap, we can arbitrarily choose a personality spectrum and outcome variable. The personality spectrum has a personality distribution. Any locus or region of the distribution we select corresponds to an outcome distribution. This distribution has an expected outcome, its average.

With that, I’ve explained my Personality Probabilistic Model (PPM), a formalization of how personality traits are distributed and how these traits affect outcomes. I recognize the following limitations of this mental model:

  • In the real world, we don’t always have sufficient data to create personality distributions and outcome distributions. Diagnostic tools are also limited in their ability to accurately quantify personality traits. Personality itself is still not a very well-understood concept, to my understanding.

  • Perhaps there’s a much more elegant or accurate expression of these same ideas in academic literature.

  • The math underlying the model can become tedious.

  • This model is difficult to explain to someone without an understanding of probability. Complexity is a possible sign of an impractical mental model.

Criticism aside, here are some potential applications of PPM:

  • Conceptualizing trends in personality traits in the population

  • Conceptualizing patterns in the relationship between personality traits and various outcomes

  • Quantifying the utility of various decisions. For example, you might estimate that A% of a group is within some range of outcome variable B. Therefore, we should spend C amount on D. At a broader level, the PPM can be used to estimate the impact of various social phenomena. Although the statistics involved are not always readily available, sometimes these quantities are estimable enough for the model to bear fruit. Furthermore, fiddling with specific quantities within the PPM can expose interesting relationships regardless.

Here’s a link to a GitHub repository containing the Python code to generate the above figures via matplotlib: PPM Repository

1

It’s unclear how SAT score correlates with IQ. I assume some association for explanatory purposes. I picked a mean value of questionable veracity based on this website and arbitrarily assumed a standard deviation of 30. I also assumed for simplicity that the outcome distribution is normal.

2

The formula I used to generate all 21 distributions is outlined in the code of the file “Figure 3.py” in the GitHub repository linked above. I arbitrarily obtained the outcome distribution corresponding to each IQ as follows:

3

The expected outcome can be obtained in two ways: 1) an arithmetic sum of the mean of each distribution (an approximation possible manually) 2) integrating over the aggregate distribution (a more precise approximation performed computationally). The file “Figure 3.py” in the GitHub repository linked above outlines these calculations more explicitly. Note that these methods only work when the outcome variable is discrete. I suspect that in continuous cases you would have to explicitly define each outcome distribution as a function of the outcome variable, then integrate over these distributions multiplied by the outcome variable.

item.title: The Metaphysics of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
item.description: This article contains MAJOR SPOILERS for the video game Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. It’s an excellent game. Go play it. You’ve been warned.
item.content:encoded:
This article contains MAJOR SPOILERS for the video game Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. It’s an excellent game. Go play it. You’ve been warned.

I love the ending of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. It’s probably the first video game I’ve played where I appreciated the lack of a definitive, happy ending. There’s so much depth to be found in Maelle and Verso’s ideological conflict at the end of the game. I’ve found myself mulling over the game’s two endings days after beating it. The dilemma of whether to allow the canvas to survive is so layered that the comprehensive discourse concerning it still hasn’t left me satisfied1.

My goal with this article isn’t to adjudicate on which of the two endings is “superior” from a moral or storytelling perspective. My honest answer to such a question—that I’m sure the developers would agree with—is that both endings are equally valid and open to interpretation. However, there’s a facet of the endings that isn’t afforded enough thought: how “real” are the people inside the canvas? More specifically, what is their moral status? I hope to contribute to this one portion of the discourse.

Verso Dessendre created the canvas the game is set in, leaving a part of his soul inside to sustain it. He painted the people of the canvas himself. There are two grounds on which to dispute the moral patienthood of the canvas people: 1) The canvas people are painted and thus not moral patients. 2) The canvas is not a “real” world because of the way it was created and exists as an extension of the “real world”. 3) Painters can manipulate canvas worlds so easily that the people they create aren’t moral patients.

My argument against the first point is that the canvas people are demonstrably equivalent to real people. They exhibit the same psychological properties as real people, such as realistic personalities, free will2, sentience, and sapience. They are also biologically identical to real people, save for perhaps their magical abilities. The fact that no one could distinguish Maelle from the canvas people is an example of this. Every characteristic I can think of that’s worthy of moral patienthood (empathy, sentience, cognitive complexity, consciousness, etc.) is present in the canvas people. The only relevant distinction is that the first canvas people were painted (and later reproduced just like real humans), while real people eventually evolved from the first organisms on Earth. I fail to see why this distinction is meaningful. Suppose you assume that only humans born from sexual reproduction (intercourse, IVF, surrogacy, etc.) are moral patients. Then you would have to defend why a human clone is not a moral patient. Otherwise, the criteria for what constitutes the legitimate creation of a human is arbitrary and thus immaterial.

I’ve established that you can’t deny the moral patienthood of canvas people on the basis of how they were created. The second argument against their moral patienthood is that the canvas is not a real world. This is a weak argument because moral patienthood is premised on the traits of an organism. Whether the canvas is real shouldn’t matter. It would be like learning that there are organisms living on Mars identical to humans and denying them moral patienthood because they don’t exist on Earth. One counterargument is that the physical separation of Earth and Mars is more real than the magical spatio-temporal separation of the canvas and the game’s version of Earth. The argument here is that physical separation is more “real” because it’s founded in real-world science. Except that the real world of Expedition 33 doesn’t follow real-world science. This is yet another arbitrary distinction.

So it seems we can’t argue that the way in which the canvas exists denies its people of moral patienthood. Well, the painters are capable of creating countless worlds of canvas people and manipulating their realities with ease. Doesn’t that strip canvas people of their moral patienthood? I disagree. Humans control the lives of farmed animals almost as freely as painters could manipulate canvases. Does that free farmed animals of moral patienthood? Of course not. The intuition here is that people in the real world exist more independently, free of magical manipulation, and are therefore more deserving of moral patienthood. The intuition falls apart when you consider that moral patienthood isn’t premised on how “difficult” it is to affect the populations of an organism.

As you can see, the canvas people ought to be afforded the same moral patienthood as real humans. I’d like to offer some additional intuitions as to why:

  1. If you were told that our world was a canvas, would that make it any less morally relevant?

  2. Would our lives cease to matter if there was a God who could substantially manipulate reality?

  3. The difference between an AI-simulated person and a canvas person is that AI behaves very differently from humans, while canvas people behave seemingly identically.

1

I highly recommend this video as the most exhaustive analysis of the endings.

2

This is evinced by the ability of the canvas people to defeat the Paintress.

item.title: Mystery Curves
item.description: A powerful mental model for storytelling.
item.content:encoded:
In stories with a mystery component, there’s a pace at which information is revealed. The relationship between the duration of the story and the proportion of information revealed can be represented by what I call the mystery curve.

In the example above, only 20% of the information in the story is revealed by its halfway point. Then the next quarter of the story contains all of its remaining revelations. Admittedly, there is no objective measure of “information revealed” in a story and there certainly isn’t a need to sketch a mystery curve when writing a story. That said, while I’m no arbiter of storytelling, I think it’s useful to model the pace of story revelations as a mystery curve. I can’t even list how many times I felt a story do a lore dump or place a big twist at the wrong time. This is where mystery curves come in handy; they help outline the flow of a story’s key mysteries.

Here are some common types of mystery curves I’ve observed in fiction:

The Endgame Lore Dump is a mystery curve structure where much of the key information in a story is rapidly revealed during its homestretch.

The Turning Point is a structure where the amount of information revealed ‘spikes’ at a turning point in the story. Unlike in the Endgame Lore Dump, the spike occurs well before the end of the story.

The Linear Structure occurs when information is revealed at a fairly consistent pace throughout the story.

The Little to No Mystery structure occurs when most of the information in a story is known from the beginning.

The Loose Ends structure occurs when not all information about the story is known by the end (notice the vertical axis of the graph ends at 80%). Think unresolved plot threads or details left deliberately ambiguous.

We can sophisticate mystery curves to reflect both the information revealed and the scope of potential information revealed (i.e. what the audience thinks they’ll come to know).

In the above chart, information scope refers to what percentage of information across the entire story the audience expects to have experienced. For example, by the halfway point, the reader of a fantasy novel might think that the protagonist will achieve their goal of exploring their entire planet. Then a twist is revealed that there’s actually a second planet to explore, meaning there’s actually another half to the story. This means that unlike mystery curves that represent information revealed, mystery curves that represent the information scope are not necessarily monotonically increasing. In lay terms, information revealed can only increase as a story progresses. However, it’s possible that partway through a story, the reader goes from thinking they know 50% of the story to thinking they know only 20% of it.

The difference between the information scope and the information revealed, which I dub an information gap, is another complex balancing act. In a small information gap, the audience believes they know everything. In a large information gap, the audience believes they know nothing, perhaps overwhelmingly so. One could plot the information gap to more explicitly visualize it (I refrain from doing so here).

There’s a wide spectrum of mystery curve structures across stories, with no story perfectly adhering to a single one. Additionally, there is no “best” mystery curve; storytellers should tailor the pace of information revealed to their story. It can also come down to personal preference. I personally prefer stories with Linear or Turning Point mystery curves and an information gap that vacillates between zero and fairly low quantities.

item.title: Can Children's Media Have Moral Ambiguity?
item.description: I’ve noticed that children’s media often either: 1) portrays its entire cast as good or 2) divides its cast into clear good and evil sides.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve noticed that children’s media often either: 1) portrays its entire cast as good or 2) divides its cast into clear good and evil sides. This is partially due to the difficulty of writing moral ambiguity and the simple fact that not all stories need to have moral ambiguity. Notwithstanding, moral clarity (as opposed to moral ambiguity) feels especially prevalent in media targeted at adults. Indeed, I can name countless popular adult shows that emphasize moral ambiguity: Breaking Bad, Better Call Saul, Dexter, Mr. Robot, Invincible, Game of Thrones, etc. However, although plenty of kids shows have some moral ambiguity, I struggle to think of ones that emphasize it. Avatar the Last Airbender explores some moral nuances well, but the show still arguably asserts clear moral stances. And ATLA is the exception, not the norm.

So why is moral ambiguity more prominent in adult shows? My proposed explanation is that kids shows aim to teach children clear morals. To see why, consider which of the two lessons is more suitable for children: 1) Here’s how to be a good guy. Here’s how to be a bad guy. Be good and not bad. 2) The world is morally complex. While you should strive for good, it’s not always easy to tell what is ‘good’ or ‘bad’.

Even as someone reluctant to patronize kids, the first approach feels a lot safer. Teaching kids objective values lays groundwork for a more sophisticated conception of morality later in life. Suppose instead that kids start to spend their early childhood hearing morally ambiguous stories. Let’s rewrite The Three Little Pigs as an example:

Once upon a time, there were three little pigs. The pigs stole money from a kind, hardworking wolf who was already struggling to feed his pups. The three pigs used the wolf’s hard-earned money to construct houses of straw, wood, and brick, respectively. The wolf’s pups were now sick from malnutrition. The wolf begged the pigs one by one for his money back. They refused. And so, he slaughtered them one by one, feeding his famished children their flesh. The end.

Was there a clear ‘good guy’ or ‘bad guy’ in the story? A morally superior side? Whether there was a morally obvious decision for either the wolf or the pigs is moot; could the average young child come away from this story with some edification? Or rather, might they think that killing those who have wronged you is justifiable? Although I’m admittedly not drawing from any empirical evidence, I believe most young children don’t possess sufficient media literacy for morally ambiguous narratives; the ambiguity of morality begets ambiguity in the lessons learned.

This is not to say that children should never be introduced to morally ambiguous stories.

In fact, the majority of my own conception of morality was shaped by the stories I enjoyed throughout my formative years. To suggest otherwise—to confine storytelling to moral clarity—could possibly atrophy people’s society’s moral faculties. My suggestion is that society gradually introduces children to media in increasing levels of moral complexity while encouraging them to process media critically.

But what should a storyteller do when tasked to tailor a story to children? Strip it of moral ambiguity? Make every character both morally good and morally complex (as is most easily done in realistic fiction)? I’m not sure. I’m genuinely not sure how to resolve this conundrum without compromising on thematic depth.
