item.title: The Button Problem
item.description: I devised a thought experiment that I call “The Button Problem”.
item.content:encoded:
I devised a thought experiment that I call “The Button Problem”. It goes like this:

Imagine that you’re given a magic button at this exact moment in time. Let’s call this time t. From now on, whenever you press the button, time is rewound back to t. Everything is reverted back to how it was, except you retain your memories. Only you can press the button and it has unlimited uses. It cannot disappear from you until the instant you die. After you die, the universe resumes onward without ever resetting again.

For example, you could rob a store, press the button, and rewind to t as though nothing happened. You could spend decades researching the cure to cancer and press the button after reaching old age to buy yourself more time. The potential practical applications are endless. Of more interest to me, however, is the moral implications of such a button—implications that make me question the intrinsic value of human experiences.

Pain in a Vacuum—The Problem of Moral Patienthood

One such implication is the idea that when you press the button is morally significant. Suppose you kill an innocent person, for instance. Is waiting 1 year to press the button morally worse than waiting 1 day to press it? I see two intuitions:

Intuition 1: The murder is morally irrelevant because the world is reset regardless. Any concomitant suffering is effectively erased.

Intuition 2: The relative amounts of pain following the murder are morally significant, despite the reset of the universe.

I assume that if you espouse Intuition 1, you believe that suffering is only relevant insofar as its consequences on the world. I disagree with this intuition. It suggests that a genocide is only a moral atrocity insofar as it harms other living humans. It suggests that a sudden, painless extinction of all of humanity is morally acceptable.

I see two arguments for Intuition 2. The first is simply that waiting one year causes more societal harm; after one day, the victim’s loved ones may not even be aware of their bereavement. In contrast, one year of grief inflicts enormous emotional harm. The second argument for this intuition is that the longer you wait after pressing the button, the higher your likelihood of death (recall that the button ceases to work after you die). We can represent this idea in terms of expected utility:

We have shown that the expected utility of never pressing the button (the left term) is greater than the expected utility of pressing it (the right term). Note that this only holds1 for a positive probability of dying before pressing the button (i.e. P(Ω ≤ τ) > 0).

This notion that the risk of not pressing the button makes murder wrong extends to all kinds of risks. Beyond the risk of death and the subsequent inability to press the button, there’s a risk of one’s values changing. Perhaps you eventually decide to keep living in this timeline where you murdered someone instead of resetting it.

Thus, we’ve established multiple arguments concerning the initial dilemma: Does the time after which you press the button matter?

To help or not to help—The Problem of Social Optimization

With the power of the button comes unlimited potential to mold society. You could use knowledge of the future to help world leaders avert catastrophes. You could replicate future inventions. You could effectively achieve immortality and leverage it to accumulate countless lifetimes’ worth of skills. But where does the desire to shape the universe end?

First, is it moral to use this power to influence society? One could argue that no individual should control such a uniquely transformative capability. I’m not entirely convinced with such a lofty ideal. In my opinion, the world is better off without certain kinds of suffering—some of which is preventable via the button. A good example of this is using prescience to alert authorities of imminent natural disasters or unequivocally harmful crimes. The merit in button-empowered changes to the future is not always so clear, however. For example, you could exploit your prescience to sway the outcome of an election. Is that morally permissible? What if you used your prescience to exploit the stock market, thereby tampering with the returns of other investors? Is that morally permissible? Is it morally permissible if you donated your astronomical returns to charity?

A comforting resolution to this dilemma is not to use the button at all. Why interfere? This is a naive resolution; the world in which you evacuate additional people from a national disaster or prevent a murder is all but objectively a superior one. There’s an opportunity cost to indifference in the form of preventable, astronomical levels of suffering.

Variations

Consider the implications of the following variations of the Button Problem on both moral patienthood (What is the morality of how we treat lives when the Button exists?) and social optimization (How should we use the Button to optimize social welfare?):

  • What if the Button had finite uses?

  • What if the Button permanently ceased to work after any button press, independently, with some probability β?

  • What if you could choose to reset the universe to any time, t’, in its history.

  • What if there were costs to each use of the Button?:

    • What if a random person died counterfactually (died in an accident as opposed to passing away naturally) after resetting the universe?

Any combination of the above variations presents a fascinating problem involving utility theory, welfare economics, population ethics, moral philosophy, and time discounting. I plan to explore these variations in a future article.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

Otherwise we have that the expected utility is equal across both cases.

item.title: A Personal Resolution of Population Ethics
item.description: Note: I realized in retrospect that the philosophy I propose of “concave average utilitarianism” already exists and is called average prioritarianism.
item.content:encoded:
Note: I realized in retrospect that the philosophy I propose of “concave average utilitarianism” already exists and is called average prioritarianism.

For those unfamiliar with the philosophical field of population ethics, I recommend the following articles as a background for the proceeding discussion:

  1. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/repugnant-conclusion/

  2. https://utilitarianism.net/population-ethics/

This article will contain rigorous mathematical definitions for the sake of formalism and clarity. That said, I’ve included non-mathematical descriptions of the proceeding mathematical definitions to (hopefully) avoid alienating less mathematically inclined readers.

Introduction

Population ethics is one of my favorite fields of philosophy due to its relevance to the Effective Altruism movement and meta-ethics at large. This post isn’t a hubristic attempt to ‘solve’ a philosophical problem that has stumped brilliant philosophers; rather, it’s an attempt for me, a moral anti-realist, to establish a theory of population ethics consistent with my moral intuitions.

The validity of any theory of population ethics is really just its consistency with certain axioms. In this sense, the field of population ethics is ‘unsolvable’: the solution is contingent on axioms derived from subjective moral intuitions, as opposed to moral facts.

Assumptions

I make the following fundamental assumptions, which are merely preliminaries for studying population ethics, as opposed to subjective moral intuitions:

  1. Each individual i in a population P has some welfare w_i in R (the set of all real numbers)1. Let W := (w_1, w_2, …, w_n) contain the welfare values of each individual in P. For example, we could have a population P = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and W = (4, –7, 0, 10, –3, 6).

  2. Comparability: Welfare values are comparable across all individuals and across different populations. Equivalently, individuals are afforded equal moral consideration.

  3. Independence: Individuals don’t influence the welfare of others2.

  4. Finiteness: P is finite3. In other words, we can’t have an infinitely large population.

  5. Valence symmetry: For every positive welfare value, there is a negative welfare value of the same magnitude4.

  6. Neutral value: There exists a neutral welfare value 0 representing a life neither worth living nor not worth living.

I use graphs of the following form for explanatory purposes:

The horizontal axis represents population size, while the vertical axis represents welfare. The blue boxes denote Population A. The height and width of each box denote the respective size and welfare of its corresponding segment of Population A. I omit specific numerical labels for height and width because these exact quantities aren’t necessary for illustrative purposes.

My proposed theory of population ethics attempts to reconcile the following population ethical intuitions:

  1. Reducing suffering >> increasing happiness: Reducing the magnitude of suffering is valued much more heavily than increasing happiness. For example, an increase from welfare -10 to welfare -5 is preferable to an increase from welfare 5 to welfare 10. This is consistent with the idea of diminishing marginal utility. Intuitively, going from destitution to mild poverty does more for a person’s welfare than going from middle-class to upper-middle-class.

    Figure 2 above shows the difference between a world where suffering was reduced (Population A) and a world where the happiness of the happy was doubled (Population B).5

  2. Population size is irrelevant: Additional happy lives lived are not intrinsically good. This directly obeys the intuition of neutrality. I further concede that additional unhappy lives lived are not intrinsically bad.

    Under this assumption, we are indifferent between Population A and Population B in Figure 3.

I discard the following population ethical intuitions:

  1. Egalitarianism: Equality in welfare among individuals does not inherently make one population preferable to another.

  2. Total Utilitarianism: To reiterate, additional happy lives lived are not intrinsically good and additional unhappy lives lived are not intrinsically bad.

Concave Average Utilitarianism

In non-mathematical terms, we can assign higher weightage to lower, negative welfare values than to higher, positive welfare values. The population with a mean welfare is then considered better.

Let’s look at an example.

What allows this theory to remain intact is the crux that the addition of unhappy lives is not intrinsically bad. This is a very powerful assumption to make because we can easily construct a population where birthing an individual of negative welfare actually increases the population’s concave average welfare. We can similarly construct a population of entirely happy people such that adding a relatively less happy still having positive welfare would lower the value of the population.

While this ‘feels’ intuitive to me, I can understand why some might disagree. Here we return (and arguably succumb) to a foundational characteristic of meta-ethics, that conclusions are heavily contingent on arbitrary moral intuitions (in the case of moral anti-realism) or moral uncertainties (in the case of moral realism).

I’m afraid I can’t offer much consolation here.

A Preference Baseline

I also devised a sufficient condition for population preferences that holds up under every typical intuition of population ethics. Suppose without loss of generality that Population A is larger than Population B.

In non-mathematical terms, we want to map each member of Population A to a member of Population B who is better off. We then check if the remaining members of Population B are better off than every member of Population A.

In Figure 4, Population A is denoted in purple and Population B is denoted in blue. A is the larger population. By ‘superimposing’ B on A, we can map each segment of Population B with a more well off segment of Population A. The rightmost purple block left over after this mapping is taller than the red line, which denotes the maximum welfare attained by an individual of Population B. Thus, under the Preference Baseline, we conclude that Population A is preferred to Population B under any typical intuitions of population ethics. This generality is the strength of the Preference Baseline, although it requires very strong conditions. Essentially, the Preference Baseline only holds when one population is better than another in every conceivable way.

Narrowing the definition of the preference baseline can yield sufficient conditions for population preferences under more specific theories of population ethics. The following condition, for instance, is sufficient to establish preferences under average utilitarianism:

In non-mathematical terms, we want to map each member of Population A to a member of Population B who is better off. We then check if the remaining members of Population B are better off than the average member of Population A.

Observe that the preference requirements under a particular theory of population ethics (average utilitarianism in this case) are looser than those of the Preference Baseline. Informally, the ‘unmapped leftovers’ of Population B must have welfare greater than the mean welfare of Population A, as opposed to the maximum welfare of Population A.

Conclusion

Thus, I’ve devised a theory of population ethics consistent with all of my intuitions, my controvertible assumptions notwithstanding.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

I couldn’t write w_i and R as mathematical symbols because Substack only allows LaTeX in blocks instead of inline symbols. The alternative was write most if not all of this post in LaTeX and either attach the file hereto or paste images of its content. I decided against this because the majority of the post is text anyways.

2

In the real world, happier people might improve the welfare of sad people. Furthermore, a larger population might have a higher average welfare by leveraging economies of scale, network effects, etc. We ignore such implications here.

3

I’m not sure how to extend population ethics to populations of infinite size. I might explore this in a future post.

4

This might seem trivial because it’s an inherent property of the real numbers (e.g. 9 has the same magnitude of -9). However, what if we applied a weightage of -1 + e^w_i to negative welfare values? Then we would have no negative welfare values weighted less than -1.

5

Some of you may have noticed that Population A appears to be smaller because Population B has two boxes of equal width to the width of Population A’s box. That’s because half of A’s population has welfare zero. I chose not to specify this because the distinction between eliminating the suffering half of the original population and increasing their welfare to zero is immaterial.

item.title: Media Realism
item.description: Moral realism is the idea that there are objective moral facts and/or truths.
item.content:encoded:
Moral realism is the idea that there are objective moral facts and/or truths. To many, it’s not a particularly crazy stance. After all, to reject moral realism, you would have to concede that the denunciation of putative moral atrocities like slavery, genocide, and torture is not on the basis of fact.

I see a similar phenomenon in media discourse. When people discuss films, for example, it’s almost reflexive to ‘appraise’ the film—to talk about artistic media as if it’s either ‘good’ or ‘bad’. It’s also common for people to assert that some films are so good or bad that they are ‘objectively good’ or ‘objectively bad’. This is all too similar to how we discuss morality: in objective good and objective bad.

I call this media realism. Media realism is belief in at least one of the following:

  1. There are objectively good pieces of media.

  2. There are objectively bad pieces of media.

  3. All media possesses some true level of objective quality.

I’m frankly irritated that these three beliefs underpin virtually all media discussion I see. In an attempt to shift media discourse away from appraisals of quality, I argue for media anti-realism, the rejection of media realism. In other words, I believe that media lacks objective quality and that it’s therefore impossible to compare pieces of media on some notion of ‘objective quality’.

My main argument is that objective quality doesn’t exist. Obviously it doesn’t exist in a scientific sense. I mean that it also doesn’t exist in an artistic sense.

For one, it’s impossible to rigorously define objective quality. Suppose, for instance, that good pacing is an indicator of objective quality of TV shows. What exactly does ‘good pacing’ mean? That well-paced TV shows adhere to certain principles? Any sensible definition of good pacing, when applied to a TV show by multiple people, would not result in the same assessment of good pacing. For good pacing to be an indicator of objective quality of TV shows, the presence or level of ‘good pacing’ in a TV show should not depend on the opinion of the observer. It would be like if the temperature of a liquid depended on who was reading the thermometer.

So it’s impossible to rigorously define objective quality. But what if it still exists, despite the impossibility of its definition? Surely there are facts of our world that exist despite the impossibility of defining them. In such a case, perhaps we can narrow the definition of objective quality enough to suggest a likelihood of objective quality. Maybe we can’t define objective quality rigorously, but surely signs point to its existence, right? Think of it like this: You think there’s a needle in a haystack because you felt a prick while gliding your hand through it. You reduce the haystack to a smaller pile of hay containing the sharp object. You feel the exact same prick while gliding your hand through the pile. Does that make it any more likely that the sharp object is a needle? No. Analogously, creating a loose definition of objective quality that aligns with our intuitions of what objective quality should be does not imply the factual existence of objective quality.

Counterarguments

One might rebut that media realism implies no objective difference in quality between a putative masterpiece and an artistic travesty. Isn’t it crazy to concede that The Shawshank Redemption isn’t an objectively better film than Morbius? Feel free to substitute both films for whatever media you hold in high and low regard, respectively. I don’t find this concession so crazy. There’s such a diversity in individual sensibilities that whatever one media realist holds as fact, another might dispute. I recognize that a lack of consensus doesn’t necessarily imply absence of objective quality in media. This is more to dispute the validity of intuitions surrounding media comparisons.

Another argument in favor of media realism is that, even if pieces of media lack some objective holistic level of quality, surely there are some aspects of media that possess objective quality. For example, even if the quality of various styles of prose is subjective, perhaps spelling, grammar, and punctuation are an aspect of the objective quality of a novel. I disagree even here. I’ve seen authors violate the conventions of the English language in appealing ways. But what if some methods of violation are objectively bad? Recall my claim that a lack of rigorous definition precludes the presence of objective quality. If you do believe that some violations of the English language are objectively bad, where do you draw the line? Cormac McCarthy? Substack writers who begin their sentences with conjunctions?

There are two unpleasant implications to the assertion that media lacks objective quality whatsoever:

  1. It is impossible for an artist to objectively improve because their newer art isn’t objectively better or worse than their older art.

  2. As a consequence of the previous implication, no artist is objectively better than another. Yet some artists are given enormous budgets for media production while others scrimp and struggle to get by.

My response to the first implication to reframe the notion of artistic improvement. I like to think of artistic improvement not as objective improvement, but as changes to one’s artistic ability and their oeuvre. These changes possess a subjective ‘goodness’ as opposed to an objective goodness.

If we accept that differences in the quality of pieces of media are subjective, we can easily reinterpret the second implication. Some artists’ media is regarded more highly than others’ because of superior recognition of quality as opposed to quality itself. I acknowledge that this is perhaps a depressing reality of creating art.

Does It Really Matter?

I would argue that even if pieces of media possess objective quality, it doesn’t matter anyways. We’ll never find a clear consensus as to what constitutes objective quality. Furthermore, artists can reframe ‘objective improvements’ to pieces of media as modifications in pursuit of a subjective target.

My Proposition

We return to the motivation behind this article: how can we shift media discourse away from appraisals of quality and, more broadly, improve media discourse?

Instead of appraising pieces of media or even classifying their characteristics on some scale of quality, we should more holistically and fundamentally discuss them. For example, instead of saying “Dark Souls 3 has a poison swamp area that’s miserable to traverse,” I could say: “Here’s how the poison swamp in Dark Souls 3 is and here’s how it made me feel.”

Furthermore, discussions of pieces of media need not touch the notion of objective or subjective quality at all. Often, my favorite discussions of pieces of media are analyses, theories, philosophical debates, and bonding over the emotional experiences media can produce.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

item.title: Cognitive Challenges
item.description: Have you ever struggled to comprehend a concept?
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever struggled to comprehend a concept? I’ve found that during such experiences, I can identify patterns in the issue of comprehension I’m facing. For example, it might be that I’m struggling to view multiple related concepts in the same picture, so to speak. I call these patterns of failed understanding cognitive challenges and attempt to categorize them in the context of pure math1, though this should translate well to virtually any field of human knowledge. I also suggest some remedies based on personal experience2. Note that there are no formal mathematical prerequisites to this article.

Volume

Sometimes a difficulty of comprehension arises from the sheer volume of content. Take this example, which uses fictive mathematical terminology:

Even if you found it easy to comprehend all three of the bolded terms above, you likely found it increasingly difficult to comprehend the exposition as a whole. I suspect that volume as a cognitive challenge arises from the limitations of working memory in encoding information (speculation on my part as a layperson).

I’ve found it helpful to separate voluminous information into classifications, to selectively retain/ignore portions of information, or to more broadly fit the information into some kind of internal structure3.

Nesting

Nesting is a cognitive challenge, adjacent to volume, that arises from the interconnection of concepts. Take the following example (don’t feel the need to read all of it):

A utility function describes a consumer’s preferences—what combinations of goods they like more than others—without yet considering any limits. Once prices and income are introduced, those preferences interact with a budget constraint, and the resulting optimal choice is the consumer’s Marshallian demand: what they actually buy when trying to do as well as possible given what they can afford. After this choice is made, we can evaluate how well off the consumer is by looking at the indirect utility, which records the level of satisfaction achieved when the consumer responds optimally to prices and income. We can then reverse the problem and ask not how much utility can be obtained from a given income, but how much income is required to obtain a given level of utility; this leads to the expenditure function, which tells us the minimum spending needed to reach a target level of satisfaction at given prices. The specific bundle that achieves this target utility at the lowest possible cost is the Hicksian demand. In this way, all of these concepts are nested around the same core preferences: utility defines what is desirable, Marshallian demand shows the best affordable choice, indirect utility measures the resulting satisfaction, expenditure asks for the cheapest way to reach a given satisfaction, and Hicksian demand identifies the cost-minimizing bundle that does so.

This AI-generated paragraph describes a set of closely related concepts in microeconomic theory: Marshallian demand, indirect utility, the expenditure function, and Hicksian demand.

Similar to volume, nesting challenges our memory. However, additionally, it demands that we understand connections between abstract entities in addition to the entities themselves. To illustrate this, suppose there are 5 distinct nodes whose properties you must memorize. Now suppose you must memorize the connection that can be drawn between any two nodes. There are 5 choose 2, or 10 connections to memorize. That’s 15 total ‘things’ to memorize.

If we increase the node count to 6, there are 15 connections and 21 things to memorize. At 10, there are 55 things to memorize. At 100 there are 4950. You get the idea. For the mathematically curious, we generalize this idea below:

Delineation

Delineation is the cognitive challenge of outlining every possibility. For example, if you flip a fair coin 5 times, you may want to outline every possible combination of outcomes. At only 5 flips, it’s feasible to draw a tree diagram or list every combination. But what if we increase the number of flips to 100? Here, delineation limits the brute force approach of outlining the problem. However, we can use set notation to explicitly define the set of possibilities.

As you can see, delineation often requires us to devise more scalable tools for comprehension. Unfortunately, this is much easier said than done. What happens when there are many abstract entities with their own sets of possibilities?

A good example of this is the definition of compactness of a set (it’s sadly difficult for me to offer a more lay-friendly example): A set X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover. Delineating the notion of compactness requires us to delineate multiple interconnected concepts (hence nesting is also present here):

  1. What are the different kinds of sets?

  2. What are possible open sets?

  3. What are possible open covers of sets?

  4. What are possible finite subcovers of sets?

Trying to simultaneously conceptualize this aggregate delineation (i.e. possible compact sets) was, at least to me, difficult at first exposure.

Compactness is an example of delineation involving multiple interrelated concepts.

You may have realized that notions of infinity can greatly complicate demarcation; when the set of possibilities is infinite, it’s difficult to conceptualize. Fortunately, instead of outlining every possibility, it might suffice to outline a relevant subset of possibilities. For example, we might only examine more common examples of compact sets. Another approach is to understand the general ‘structure’ of an infinite set of possibilities. An example of this is how we graph functions on the coordinate plane with arrows to denote an infinite domain.

Pattern Recognition

Sometimes no amount of memorization or familiarity guarantees that one knows the solution to a math problem. Sometimes one needs to know how to reframe or discern subcomponents of a problem. This, in essence, is pattern recognition. It’s a cognitive challenge discoverable even outside of math and is difficult to describe.

Compression

Compression is condensation of multiple mathematical steps or implications into a single step. An example of this is making multiple arithmetic simplifications in a single step when showing your work. Performing greater degrees of compression requires greater mathematical proficiency. Similarly, when reading math, such as a proof, comprehending more compressed steps requires more mathematical proficiency. Compression is present everywhere outside of math as well: in our vocabulary, social behavior, etc—so much so that it warrants its own article.

Notation

Notation is an extension of compression. Addition is a compression of counting. Multiplication is a compression of addition. Exponentiation is a compression of multiplication. You get the idea. Mathematical notation concisely expresses a compression of concepts. The difficulty is that this compression can introduce both volume and nesting. One non-mathematical analogue for notation is jargon.

Conclusion

Cognitive challenges manifest in multifarious forms across all fields of human knowledge. Although they make learning more difficult, this merely a reflection of the complexity of reality itself.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

I chose pure math because it entails thinking at the most fundamental level and has given rise to every cognitive challenge I enumerate.

2

I’m not sure to what extent cognitive scientists have already formalized what I describe here.

3

For example, if you’re trying to comprehend the stages of an animal’s life cycle, you don’t have to memorize them all individually. You can draw connections from one stage to a subsequent stage.

item.title: Compression in Society
item.description: In my most recent article, I coined the term cognitive challenges. Cognitive challenges are patterns that make information more difficult to comprehend. For example, sometimes a text introduces so many new concepts at once that it’s difficult to see the bigger picture. I previously introduced a cognitive challenge called
item.content:encoded:
In my most recent article, I coined the term cognitive challenges. Cognitive challenges are patterns that make information more difficult to comprehend. For example, sometimes a text introduces so many new concepts at once that it’s difficult to see the bigger picture. I previously introduced a cognitive challenge called compression, which is when information is condensed.

As an example, suppose you’re reading a recipe for a cake. One of the steps in the recipe instructs you to whisk cake batter. Most of us intuitively know how to whisk cake batter; we don’t have to be told every exact subsidiary action involved in whisking cake batter, like how to grab the whisk, or the stirring motion to use. This is compression—the idea that we can condense the minute details of what ‘whisking’ is in order to avoid overcomplicating the cake recipe.

Compression is omnipresent in society. Informational texts, such as recipes, expect a level of prerequisite knowledge. Some of these prerequisites are so elementary that they’re almost universally a part of our knowledge system and thus difficult to even discern as compression. A cooking recipe need not warn you not to touch a hot stove—it’s something humans almost universally learn at a young age. The term ‘common sense’ also reflects a type of compression in our society. Common sense broadly encompasses intuitions like not touching dirty objects and maxims like offering condolences to a recently bereaved friend.

It makes sense that society performs compressions of information. Could you imagine having to convey all information as exhaustively as possible? Like axioms? Maybe it’s impossible to avoid any manner of compression. Language, our premier communicative tool, is inherently compressive. When we point to a certain fruit and call it an ‘apple,’ we’re communicating a complex identification of multifarious observations, like the shape of the fruit and its color. Our vision operates under compression; it makes visual categorizations and leverages heuristics. I’m no neuroscientist, but I’d wager that even our thoughts are compressions of sensory information. Thus, compression is ineluctable.

Compression can have major repercussions. First, compression results in inevitable miscommunication. No matter how eloquently I attempt to write this article, for instance, no one will comprehend it in the same manner in which I do. The consequences of these kinds of misunderstandings range as broadly from international conflict to a disappointed reader of my Substack. Second, in a similar light, compression renders it impossible to perceive the world with perfect objectivity; the condensation of sensory information introduces subjectivity and illusions.

Fortunately, compression bestows several benefits as well. First, compression streamlines communication1. Textbook authors can actually finish writing during their sabbaticals by omitting a comprehensive solutions manual. Substack writers, perhaps at least a little conceited, can neglect to provide a lengthy list of examples. Teachers can avoid having to walk students through details taught in prerequisite classes. Second, compression allows us to comprehend information better by condensing it in effective ways. Mnemonics, acronyms, and notes are all examples of this.

Finally, there’s an artistic beauty to the imperfections and subjectivity compression introduces to our world. Take the novel Animal Farm. It uses a story about farm animals as an allegory for communist ideology. Picture that there is some ‘true’ notion of communism and that Animal Farm’s portrayal condenses this notion. Compression enables diverse interpretations of informational and creative works. This breeds political partisanship, religious fundamentalism, and misinformation. Yet, it also allows us to engage with art and to embrace the diverse intellectual backgrounds people come from.

Compression is a cognitive challenge that can make understanding a homework assignment a Herculean task. But beyond its definition, it’s interwoven into the fabric of our society.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

Daniel Kahneman discusses an analogous idea of ‘System 1’ in his book Thinking Fast and Slow.

item.title: The Game Theory of Social Interaction
item.description: Disclaimer: I’m not an expert on game theory or economics.
item.content:encoded:
Disclaimer: I’m not an expert on game theory or economics. If I made a mistake, please let me know.

Social interaction is full of uncertainty. When meeting someone for the first time, venturing to make a certain kind of joke can cause great offense or spark a deeper connection. Life is full of social interactions like these, where individuals have a set of actions that yield different outcomes depending on what those around them choose. We consider these possible outcomes in order to interact with each other strategically. This is the essence of a field of economics called game theory. I’ll proceed to use game theory to both cerebrally examine social interactions1 and introduce some of you to game theory in a lay-friendly manner.

Formal vs. Informal

Suppose you meet a guy named John Nash for the first time at a party. You can either behave formally or informally. Similarly, John can either behave formally or informally. Each of you would love to skip the formalities, so ideally, both of you opt for informal behavior. It’s not so simple, however. If one of you behaves formally and the other behaves informally, the person behaving informally will suffer embarrassment—the absolute worst possible experience a human can suffer—while the other person experiences a pleasant ego boost. If both of you behave formally, you won’t have much fun, but you won’t endure embarrassment either. Here’s a visual representation of the scenario:

The rows represent the actions you can take, while the columns represent the actions John Nash can take. In each quadrant of the 2 x 2 matrix is an ordered pair, where the first value denotes your utility payoff and the second value denotes John’s utility payoff. Think of utility as how much more or less happy you become2. You want to maximize utility. You guys each choose in your head, so it’s not possible for either of you to know ahead of time what the other person chose.

Herein lies the complexity of the interaction3 that game theory is equipped to tackle. Suppose John Nash behaves informally. Then you’re strictly better off by behaving formally (the ego boost yields higher utility for you than hitting it off with him). Suppose instead that John behaves formally. Then you’re again strictly better off by behaving formally (you want to avoid the humiliation of seeming frivolous). It seems that whether John behaves formally or informally, you gain more utility from behaving formally. In this scenario, we call behaving formally a dominant strategy and behaving informally a dominated strategy. A dominant strategy is an action that makes you better off than any other available action, regardless of what the other person does. Inversely, a dominated strategy is an action that makes you worse off than some other action, regardless of what the other person does.

You choose to behave formally because it’s a dominant strategy for you. John is a strategically-minded guy who will take the action that maximizes his utility; more formally, we say that John is rational. John can deduce that you’ll always behave formally. Given that you behave formally, he gains more utility from behaving formally than from behaving informally. Thus, you both behave formally and are both worse off than you would be if both of you behaved informally. The combination of both of your decisions to behave formally is called a Nash equilibrium (NE) in game theory. A Nash equilibrium is a combination of people’s actions such that neither player could gain higher utility from changing their action; if you change to behave informally while John behaves formally, you’re worse off. Similarly, if John changes to behave informally while you behave formally, he’s worse off.

This NE might seem to produce a stupid outcome. I, as an enjoyer of game theory, agree. Why can’t you and John Nash both just joke around with each other instead of playing these selfish games? The answer is that, in game theory, people take the action that maximizes their own utility. You and John are selfish actors. Therefore, each of your individual actions make sense. These kinds of strategic scenarios, called games, might seem useless. After all, people in real life don’t always have egos. They don’t always behave selfishly. We have social norms in place to induce certain patterns of behavior.

Now that we’ve laid the groundwork, let’s examine some (hopefully) more useful games. The goal in modeling social interactions as games is not to claim that real people engage in these over-simplistic interactions, but to conceptualize the underlying logic of said interactions.

Is this guy a snob?

Suppose, at another party, you meet a guy named Oskar Morgenstern and begin chatting with him one-on-one. You’ve become a more humble person who no longer relishes in other people’s humiliation, which should simplify your decision of whether to behave formally or informally towards him. However, you’ve come to learn that people in this world are either snobbish or jovial; Oskar could be either. If Oskar is snobbish, you play the following game:

If this is the case, Oskar, possibly a little uptight, responds poorly to informal behavior. Oskar’s dominant strategy is to behave formally; he always earns more utility from behaving formally, regardless of what you do. You can verify for yourself that, in this case, it’s best to limit your conversation to the weather.

If, instead, Oskar is jovial, you play the following game:

Here, Oskar doesn’t detest formal behavior but is very receptive to informal behavior. You can verify for yourself that, in this case, you could indulge in a spirited discussion about personal lives, strange humor, and fringe philosophies.

Unfortunately for you, it’s unclear whether Oskar is snobbish or jovial. Let’s say that, according to your experience, there’s a probability of ϵ that he’s snobbish and 1 - ϵ that he’s jovial. I’ll avoid getting into the mathematical details of how to solve this game, though those of you familiar with Bayesian Nash equilibrium can verify my results. Here are the Nash equilibria present in the game:

  1. If ϵ < 1/3, you behave informally. If Oskar is snobbish, he behaves formally. If Oskar is jovial, he behaves informally.

  2. If ϵ > 1/3, you behave formally. If Oskar is snobbish, he behaves formally. If Oskar is jovial, he behaves informally.

  3. If ϵ = 1/3, you are indifferent between behaving formally and informally. If Oskar is snobbish, he behaves formally. If Oskar is jovial, he behaves informally.

Despite my hand-waving, these equilibria should make some sense. If Oskar isn’t likely to be snobbish, behave informally. If Oskar is likely to be snobbish, behave formally. And of course, if there’s a 1/3 change of him being formal, take your pick.

Visiting Each Other

Suppose you and your best friend John Von Neumann (JVN) live in separate apartments on the same college campus (apartments A and B, respectively). On a given day, each of you can choose to visit either apartment A or B. You both would much rather hang out together than be apart. However, you prefer for JVN to visit your apartment (A) and JVN prefers for you to visit his apartment (B). You play the following game:

Fortunately, you can both coordinate before going anywhere by calling each other. One NE is for both of you to hang out at apartment A. Another is for both of you to hang out at apartment B. There’s actually another kind of Nash equilibrium called a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium (MSNE). An MSNE is a Nash equilibrium where one or both players randomize between their strategies (e.g. play one action half the time and the other half the time). In this game, there is a MSNE where you both hang out at apartment A half of the time and hang out at apartment B half of the time4. In an MSNE, neither of you can gain more utility from visiting one of the apartments more or less than half the time. One intuitive way to think of this MSNE is that you guys would rather fairly alternate between hangout spots than spend a day alone.

Romantic Confession

Ideally, you should now see some merit in modeling social interaction, as well as strategic interactions more broadly, via a game-theoretic approach. We’ll now examine a game where people take actions sequentially as opposed to simultaneously.

Suppose you and a man named John Harsanyi5 are smitten with each other and want to start dating. Being the one who always takes initiative, you can either confess to him or not confess. If you confess to him, he may either accept or reject your confession. Here’s a visual representation of this game:

When interpreting this diagram, we begin at the top with your decision and progress along the branches corresponding to each player’s decisions. The ordered pairs at the bottom denote the utility payoffs of every possible sequence of actions, with the first value denoting your payoff and the second denoting John’s payoff. To solve this game (i.e. decide what actions each player should choose), we start at the bottom of the diagram and work our way up. Suppose you confess. John will choose to accept, because it yields him higher utility than rejecting your confession. The game reduces to this:

You obtain a higher payoff from confessing, so, as a rational6 person, you confess. This is the game’s Nash equilibrium, because no other possible action on your part could yield you higher utility. Our approach of analyzing the game by starting at the bottom and working our way up is known in game theory as backward induction; the approach of using final outcomes to ‘foresee’ the optimal strategy can be intuitively extrapolated to all kinds of social interactions.

Even if you see the merit in game theory, you may object that, in real life, you won’t always know if your crush reciprocates your feelings. Now we turn to a more realistic game. Suppose you don’t know whether John Harsanyi reciprocates your burning crush. Say he reciprocates with probability p and doesn’t reciprocate with probability 1 - p. You play the following game:

Analysis of the game reveals that you should confess if p >= 1/2 and not confess if p < 1/2. Though I won’t provide a full mathematical explanation, essentially, you should confess only if it yields higher expected utility than not confessing.

Grade Competition

In a lot of college classes, students will help a small amount of others, but nowhere close to the entire class. I hope to offer a compelling game-theoretic explanation using some math (mostly algebra, although an understanding of single-variable calculus is helpful). Although this is our first time examining a game with more than two players, we can apply the same principles already covered.

In other words, none of the students gain any utility when choosing the optimal amount of classmates to help7. This might seem silly. In the real world, students are not identical. That is, some might score above or below 70 when no one in the class helps each other. Additionally, they might observe different gains from helping their classmates instead of gains represented by some universal function g(n_i). It’s certainly possible to model these considerations, perhaps in a future article. We won’t do so here because: 1) this article has suffered from enough scope creep 2) I don’t want to assume too many knowledge prerequisites 3) I want to preserve what little remains of my sanity after the consecutive hours I’ve spent devising the assortment of aforementioned games.

You might also see that the game reduces to a problem of maximizing the gains function g(n_i). Therefore, isn’t much of the structure of the game unnecessary scaffolding? Not necessarily. We’ve captured a very valuable insight. Namely, that when utility is based on relative performance, the benefits of helping each other can cancel out. This general structure of this game can be extended to all kinds of contexts where performance is relative and individuals must weigh personal gains against collective gains. I reiterate that, crucially, it’s not necessary for this model to realistically capture all such contexts; it’s a mental model for abstraction.

Conclusion

I’ve demonstrated in (hopefully) sufficient capacity the merit in using game theory to model social interactions. Game theory’s ability to account for the strategic decisions of others can help us cut through the noise of human interaction to conceptualize more fundamental strategies, incentives, and patterns at play.

Further Reading

For those looking for a lay-friendly exposition on game theory, I recommend The Joy of Game Theory: An Introduction to Strategic Thinking by Presh Talwalkar.

For those looking for a mathematically rigorous exposition on game theory, I’ve had a generally positive experience with chapter 7 of Advanced Microeconomic Theory by Geoffrey A. Jehle and Philip J. Reny.

Depending on the reception of this article and the recovery of my sanity (game theory can be a highly engrossing intellectual rabbit hole), I may explore extensions of game-theoretic social interactions in the future.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

You’ll likely find that although the average person doesn’t consciously employ game theory in their decisions during social interactions, their subconscious decision-making somewhat aligns with game-theoretic reasoning.

This strategic interaction is called “the Prisoner’s Dilemma” in game theory.

This is because both players can coordinate. Otherwise, you choose apartment A with probability .6 and JVN chooses apartment B with probability .6.

5

I’m realizing as I write this that there are quite a few notable game theorists named ‘John’.

6

Recall that ‘rational’ has a different definition in game theory than in everyday language.

7

For those familiar with microeconomic theory: there is no corner solution, so the interior solution is symmetric.

item.title: Limitations of Development Economics
item.description: My current career goal is to become a development economist (I encourage those unfamiliar with what an ‘economist’ does to read this).
item.content:encoded:
My current career goal is to become a development economist (I encourage those unfamiliar with what an ‘economist’ does to read this). More specifically, I want to research problems in the field of development economics1 (dev econ), which studies how low- and middle-income countries can improve welfare, decrease poverty, and promote economic growth. Global poverty is one of the most salient issues humanity faces, and dev econ equips us to examine it not as impossibly complex, ineluctable suffering, but as a tractable avenue for human empowerment.

While the dev econ has proliferated through computer-enabled advancements in data science and burgeoning financial resources, it continues to face a quagmire of limitations. I, as an undergraduate student, don’t claim to have any solutions to these limitations; indeed, even preeminent development economists lack the answers, as they would otherwise popularize them. My motivation in writing this is to elucidate these limitations to invite more discourse. I classify the limitations of the field in three main categories:

  1. Methodological: limitations of the methodology of dev econ (and more broadly empirical economics)

  2. Implementation: fundamental limitations of the typical implementation of dev econ insights

  3. Unknowns: grander unsolved, scantly understood questions of dev econ

Methodological Limitations

Perhaps the most foundational limitation of development economics is the notion of poverty. Development economists’ primary objective, the alleviation of poverty, is really to systematically improve the welfare of the suffering (i.e. the poor). Human welfare is a highly complex concept and poverty is one of our best proxies for it. Unfortunately, it’s no easy task to measure poverty2.

First, at what level do we measure poverty? The individual? The household? An entire region? An entire country? At the individual level, we can use measures such as income, consumption, caloric intake, and self-reported happiness At the household level, we can use household income, household consumption3, and average self-reported happiness. At a regional or national level, we can use the Human Development Index (HDI), GDP, GDP per capita, GNP, poverty rates, mean/median income, economic growth rate, and average self-reported happiness (some of which may be subject to PPP adjustments4). I’ve listed only some of the many indicators of poverty at various scales. We typically have more data at a larger scale, but this data lacks detail. Furthermore, while larger scale poverty data can be used to establish stronger trends than small scale poverty data, in practice we can make stronger empirical claims about poverty at a more granular scale.

Second, measures of poverty come with multifarious strengths and weaknesses. GDP is commonly criticized for its incomplete accounting of non-economic forms of welfare (strong community, low violence, etc.) and economic inequality, among other objections. Although these criticisms are not without merit, GDP and its related measures are fairly encompassing indicators of nationwide human welfare. Another reason that GDP is mainstay as a measure of welfare is that it is strongly correlated with proposed alternatives (see here for a statistical explanation).

The poverty rate is yet another problematic measure of poverty. Determining poverty rates requires the imposition of a poverty line. The $1/day and $2/day poverty lines remain some of the most popular thresholds. One problem with such a poverty line is that it’s fixed and thus fails to account for income mobility (inflation adjustments merely mitigate this). We could track how income increases across income percentiles to show that even the poorest of a country are becoming richer over time (adjusting for inflation and PPP of course). This approach still doesn’t establish a poverty rate, which is useful for establishing regional variation in poverty (e.g. one province has higher rates of poverty than another).

The second problem with a poverty line is that it is somewhat arbitrary. Namely, economists subjectively assess that those below some X threshold of income experience a low enough level of welfare to be deemed ‘poor’. We could construct a ‘basket’ of ‘necessities’ and determine the requisite income to purchase the basket. Those below the threshold of requisite income are deemed poor. Unfortunately, it’s arbitrary what goods qualify as necessary, assuming we have good enough data to construct the basket in the first place.

The third problem with a poverty line is that it’s binary. According to the line, someone is either poor or not. The reality is, of course, a more nuanced spectrum. One nostrum is to divide poverty into thresholds. This method could similarly identify two people of similar income as experiencing two distinct levels of poverty. For example, suppose $2/day is the threshold between ‘extreme poverty’ and ‘moderate poverty’. Someone who earns $1.99/day is classified as categorically more poor than someone who earns $2.01/day.

We return to our discussion of the methodological limitations of measures of poverty. I conclude this discussion with a criticism of self-reported happiness as a measure of human welfare. Self-reported happiness is alluring because it purports to capture non-economic aspects of human happiness. Self-reported happiness, commonly measured on a scale from 1–10 (with a 1 being extreme misery and a 10 being pure bliss), is not all that it seems. First, it’s subject to hedonic adaptation; essentially, as your life becomes lastingly better or worse, your standards for happiness may rise or lower accordingly. Second, the 1–10 scale is limited in its range. The difference between a ‘1’ and a ‘10’ is different for, say, a well-off resident of a developed country than someone who clawed their way from destitution to the upper echelons of society. Third, there is cultural variation in what constitutes happiness, which is perhaps poetic. Finally, individuals may have inaccurate perceptions of their own happiness. What time frame does one use in determining self-reported happiness? Last week? Last month? How do we aggregate our worst and best experiences during that time frame into one quantity? What if our mood at the moment of questioning distorts self-reported happiness? There’s clearly too much noise in our assessments of our own emotions.

I now shift from criticisms of the notions of poverty and poverty measurement to a criticism of Randomized Control Trials (RCTs). For those unfamiliar with RCTs, imagine we’re testing the effect of some experimental treatment on some outcome. For example, we could test the effect of melatonin gummies on hours of sleep. We select a random sample5 of participants and randomly assign some of them the treatment. Those who receive the treatment are collectively called the treatment group, while those who didn’t receive the treatment are called the control group. In this case, those who don’t receive the melatonin gummies are the control group. Those who ingest the recommended serving of melatonin gummies every night before sleeping are the treatment group6.

RCTs, traditionally employed in medical studies, proliferated in the social sciences in the late 1990s, in what became known as the RCT Revolution. Development economics adopted RCTs because of their remarkable explanatory power. Traditionally in economics, the complexity of society introduces too many confounding variables—factors that can unknowingly distort experimental results. Economists, therefore, typically substitute the controlled experiments of natural science for clever quasi-experimental designs. RCTs were novel in that they bypassed the scourge of confounding variables. Because RCTs randomly assigned the treatment, the control group and the treatment group were virtually identical in everything besides the treatment. This effectively isolated the treatment effect, allowing for copious explanatory power. It’s easy to see why the development economics gravitated toward RCTs given their methodological simplicity and explanatory power. It sure helped that three economists, Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, and Michael Kremer, were awarded a nobel prize (more accurately the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences) in 2019 for their use of RCTs.

The reluctance to impugn RCTs is, arguably, the greatest failing of modern dev econ. For one, RCTs can lack generalizability. In the context of dev econ, the results of an RCT conducted in one country may not translate to another country. Second, RCTs are highly resource-intensive. They are seldom accessible to all but esteemed economists. Third, it’s unclear how scalable RCTs are. In other words, the effect of a treatment on a small sample scattered throughout a region may differ from the effect of the same treatment when imposed universally or much more widely throughout a region. Finally, RCTs struggle to uncover the mechanisms by which the treatment effect exists. In our hypothetical RCT, for instance, even if melatonin gummies increase hours of sleep, it’s unclear why.

In summary, efforts to measure poverty and the widespread use of the beloved RCT face serious limitations.

Implementation Limitations

Perhaps the biggest limitation in implementing knowledge from dev econ—or any field of research, for that matter—is politics. Suppose a development economist determines with strong epistemic rigor that implementing some exact policy X yields very positive results for society7. Implementing a government policy instead of, say, mobilizing private funding leverages enormous government resources and allows for a more lasting institutional change. However, implementing policy X is easier said than done. Maybe X’s implementation would require an unfeasible reallocation of government resources. Maybe X’s implementation would require the persuasion of many bureaucrats, a Herculean task if X is politically polarizing. Should X become implemented, it could be modified or repealed (like USAID).

To make matters worse, there is little trust in economists. Skeptics of economists have some valid points: the field of economics has fundamental weaknesses8, economists have repeatedly made mistakes, and society should never place too much stock in any one body of opinions in general. It’s important to note that, despite their not uncommon mistakes, economists are often our best shot at tackling complex social issues, armed with the existing body of economic literature. Great economists are besmirched by economists who, often hired by less than innocent corporations or stakeholders, distort facts to advance an agenda. This is all to say that a great number of political barriers obstruct dev econ, arguably for valid reasons at times.

One such reason is the tendency of the field of economics (not just dev econ) to neglect qualitative information in favor of quantifiable information9. The field’s emphasis on mathematical rigor enables more epistemically rigorous discovery at the expense of scathing blind spots. When quantitative methods and data quality/availability bottleneck dev econ research, qualitative knowledge may open a path forward. Two professors at my university whom I greatly admire, Dean Spears and Diane Coffey, took this to heart when conducting research for their book, Where India Goes: Abandoned Toilets, Stunted Development and the Costs of Caste. Their book opens by using exploratory data analysis to examine the unusually high rates of open defecation in India. The preliminary data analysis (a quantitative method) disproves any conventional explanation for this phenomenon (India’s developing economy, lack of education, etc.). I’m skeptical that the conventional quantitative methods of dev econ could have clarified this puzzle.

Fortunately, Dean and Diane conducted countless enlightening interviews in Uttar Pradesh (UP), one of the poorest states in India. They discovered that the issue of open defecation is entrenched in the remnants of India’s oppressive caste system. Essentially, many residents of UP cannot afford proper toilets connected to a sewage system. The best alternative is to use a latrine emptied into a large underground pit. Higher caste Indians refuse to empty such pits, insisting that it’s the duty of Dalits (the lowest caste). Dalits justifiably refuse to empty latrine pits as a form of rebellion against the caste system. Thus, it’s unfeasible for most people in rural UP to use a latrine or a toilet. These people instead defecate in the open, producing a slew of nasty public health outcomes. Dean and Diane ultimately struggled to provide a robust solution to the issue of open defecation in India, but their receptiveness to conducting qualitative research has illuminated the issue for other gumption-filled individuals to tackle.

I’ll concede that claiming “development economists should take qualitative research more seriously” is hardly actionable. How do we assess the optimal context-dependent balance between qualitative and quantitative methods? How do we avoid becoming eluded by the lack of epistemic clarity found via qualitative methods? These are tough questions that I merely hope to illuminate.

Related to the neglect of qualitative information is the pervasive ethnocentrism in dev econ. The perhaps antiquated, perhaps quixotic theory of change of dev econ envisions wealthy nations and entities throwing capital at benign economic development initiatives which eventually produce universal economic prosperity. Trust me when I say that this is the dream of virtually anyone interested in development economics. Now for some disillusionment. Trust in wealthy economic development institutions is largely a Western notion. These institutions, successes notwithstanding, have at times failed to produce significant results, been exploited by bad actors, and inadvertently caused harm. It’s easy for those of us in the ivory tower—as most development economists are10—to assume what kinds of interventions make the global poor better off. Incidentally, poor people tend to understand much better than us just what makes them better off.

One study conducted in 2017 by Sara Lowes and Eduardo Montero examines colonial-era attempts to eradicate trypanosomiasis, a common disease in Sub-Saharan Africa that can cause severe neurological damage if left untreated. French colonizers used a drug containing arsenic to treat sick villagers. The drug resulted in awful side effects such as blindness, gangrene, and death. The repercussions of adherence to Western medicine have traumatized much of the developing world, who may therefore opt for alternative medicines.

You may object that this anecdote is in the context of colonialism. Surely well-intentioned development efforts are not so misguided. Be that as it may, they are certainly still ethnocentric. One paper by Nathan Nunn describes a complex, Hindu-based irrigation system in Bali, Indonesia called Agama Tirtha. Following the Green Revolution of the 1970s, farmers who practiced Agama Tirtha were advised to abandon it in favor of more modern agricultural practices. Fields previously irrigated according to Agama Tirtha suffered from insect infestations. Ignorance towards foreign cultures is a major impediment to dev econ that we would do well to remain conscious of.

All in all, political complications, a neglect of qualitative methods, and ethnocentrism all challenge the dev econ.

Unknown Limitations

On top of all the aforementioned limitations, dev econ still lacks answers to a few foundational questions.

First, what causes economic growth?11 The short answer is that we don’t know. We have explanations of varying quality for periods of high growth in specific countries and regions of the world. There’s a burgeoning literature to explain what causes social mobility at a smaller scale (i.e. individuals, families, and neighborhoods). You could assemble a team of preeminent development economists and a repository of all available economic data, yet still fail to answer this question12. Data limitations and methodological limitations exist, sure. But the true bottleneck in progressing this question is that noteworthy episodes of economic growth are all so unique that it’s impossible to isolate their underlying causal mechanisms. Quite simply, we can’t easily extrapolate the causes of South Korea’s economic boom to Latin America.

Second, how impactful is the dev econ? Perhaps someone could estimate more highly documented fractions of this impact, such as the consequences of well-documented poverty interventions. Perhaps we can examine, case by case, the social impact of preeminent development economists. If we’re to keep investing heavily into dev econ, whether in development institutions, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), or dev econ research, we ought to rigorously and regularly assess its impact13. I’m sure various forms of what I’m describing exist. Frankly, this article has become so ambitious that I’m moving on from this question.

Finally, does economic development improve welfare? The foundational assumption of dev econ is that the answer to this question is a ‘yes’. Otherwise, the field and with it my career path are rendered immaterial. I, biased as I may be, believe that economic development tends to improve overall welfare. There may still exist exceptions, however. The most popular objection in the field is the Easterlin paradox, which finds that happiness doesn’t increase as income grows within nations. One common explanation is hedonic adaptation. Of course, the Easterlin paradox is widely disputed. A combination of intuition, personal experience, and intuition seems to suggest that many fundamental economic developments, including access to food, water, and healthcare, substantially and lastingly improve overall welfare.

I once played devil’s advocate in favor of the Easterlin paradox when discussing it with a mentor. My mentor recounted his personal experience in UP, where a development intervention spearheaded under Dean Spears allowed babies to survive when they would’ve otherwise died. His eyes glimmered as he cleared his throat to share this account; it was the most vulnerable I had ever seen him. I immediately stopped playing devil’s advocate. There are a number of reasons why it’s difficult to outright disprove the Easterlin paradox: happiness is an inscrutable, immeasurable concept, for one. There are also a number of reasons to take the Easterlin paradox seriously, foremost that it challenges the foundational assumption of dev econ and the crusade against poverty. But we may never resolve it. And that’s okay. Because when I think back to my mentor’s story and all the stories of those touched by dev econ, there’s an answer I choose to believe.

Further Reading

I only just scratched the surface of dev econ. I implore you to check out some of the following resources, whether to critique my writing, criticize dev econ, or fall in love with it even half as much as I have. In no particular order:

  1. Poor Economics by Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo

  2. Good Economics for Hard Times by Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo

  3. Where India Goes: Abandoned Toilets, Stunted Development and the Costs of Caste by Dean Spears and Diane Coffey

  4. “Between the Lines: A History of the Most Important Concept in Global Poverty” by Ranil Dissanayake

  5. “Rethinking economic development” by Nathan Nunn

  6. Happiness and Life Satisfaction (Our World in Data)

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

For example, a large tub of popcorn costs around $9 in movie theaters where I live, yet less than 100 rupees (<$2) in Hyderabad, India when I visited about two years ago. PPP calculations are obtained by construct a ‘basket of goods’ and comparing the cost of this basket across countries. The convenience of PPP adjustments is taken for granted. The calculations are difficult because there is no ‘standard’ basket of goods; some goods in one country don’t have an equivalent in another country. That said, it’s standard practice for economists to perform PPP adjustments in their research (those who don’t figuratively have tomatoes thrown at them during research seminars).

Those who can pursue a PhD in development economics and subsequently become development economists tend to come from a stronger privilege and educational background to begin with. It’s tragic that those suffering the most are often the ones least equipped to solve the issues plaguing them.

item.title: A Time Paradigm
item.description: Disclaimer: I decided against mathematically formalizing this article.
item.content:encoded:
Disclaimer: I decided against mathematically formalizing this article. As you’ll come to see, it’s too complicated to reduce from a philosophical problem to a mathematical one. There are components that can be mathematically formalized, but this is largely not worthwhile and can be done on your own.

Our life circumstances can vary wildly. Family financial situations, demographic characteristics (race, religion, height, etc.), congenital conditions, and our social environment are just some of the unfathomably complex ways in which any two individuals on Earth are dealt a different hand1. Yet, however unique our circumstances, we’re universally under the thrall of time. Even so, I’ve observed no shortage of flaws in people’s perceptions of time. It’s for this reason that here I aim to synthesize my observations into one cohesive paradigm of time.

Time Is Not Uniform

People commonly worship early risers while lamenting their own disorganized sleep schedule. This implies that not all hours in the day are created equal. To illustrate this, suppose we have two people named Hashton All and Johnny, respectively. Hashton sleeps at 8:00 pm and wakes up at 4:00 am every day. Johnny sleeps at 3:00 am and wakes up at 11:00 am every day. Both Hashton and Johnny receive 8 hours of sleep a day, but many would argue that Hashton’s sleep schedule is superior. Whether this is true, it reminds us that individual productivity levels fluctuate based on a situation in time. Think of a situation as an exact point in time as well as the context preceding it. Examples include waking up late with a hangover and spending your 30th Christmas with your newborn kids.

One fluctuation in the nature of a period of time is the kind based on the time of day. While Hashton may find his time (spent smashing expensive glass bottles of water) more productive at 3:00 am, Johnny might be more productive at night. The most common explanation for this kind of pattern is chronotypes; colloquially, this is the distinction between early birds and night owls.

Another such fluctuation is in the sequence of events. Suppose you study for a math test at 1:00 pm for exactly one hour. The productivity of this studying might hinge on how full or empty your stomach is; food comas and hunger can make for some significant distractions. This sequence need not be limited to the span of a single day. Maybe you earned a job promotion yesterday, which motivates you to work even harder the next day.

We’ve established that the nature of any interval of time varies by its situation: both the interval’s exact point in time (e.g. 1/15/26 from 9:00 pm to 9:30 pm) and the sequence of events preceding the interval (e.g. if your grandma passed away a few hours ago). Thus, at risk of oversimplifying, any rational person will simultaneously:

  1. Determine tasks that are an optimal uses of time, sort of like devising an agenda or a to-do list.

  2. Apportion this agenda into time intervals2 (e.g. I need to study for an hour and spend 15 minutes vacuuming).

  3. Sequence these time intervals (e.g. I should study for an hour before playing video games for an hour).

We’ll call any particular set of time intervals and their arrangement as schedule. This time optimization problem is rife with uncertainty and cognitive complexity, so we make our best estimates and approximations using heuristics. For example, if you know that you should eat three meals at X, Y, and Z times every day, this constraint reduces the relevant spectrum of possible agendas for the day; if I want to run and there’s only one hour in the day where it’s practical for me to do so, then that simplifies my time optimization problem.

The existence of components 2. and 3. of the time optimization problem implies that time is not uniform. Think of it this way: if time was uniform, then I could inconsequentially rearrange time intervals. I could, for example, reallocate the next week’s worth of meals to this week. I could then pig out all of this week and fast all of next week. The uniformity of time would imply that this is equivalent to a more normal diet.

Time Doesn’t Transform Well

When I say that time doesn’t transform well, I mean that applying certain kinds of transformations to an interval of time has ramifications. Here are some examples of transformations:

  1. Scaling: Scaling stretching or shrinking of a time interval. It includes truncation, the removal of one or more of the components of the interval entirely, and elongation, the addition of one or more components to the interval. Suppose you plan to study for a test for an hour. If we were to increase or decrease the duration of this interval, it would come with ramifications. First, a long time spent studying without a substantial break has diminishing returns3. Second, it takes time to enter a ‘flow state’. If you decrease the duration of the interval, thus studying for less time, you risk learning less per unit of time spent. In this particular case, because the returns of studying to time are ‘S-shaped’ (i.e. you enter a flow state, then begin to plateau in productivity), we cannot scale this time interval by some factor X and expect X times as much yield. More generally, scaling doesn’t have ‘well-behaved’ properties.

  2. Shifting: Shifting is the movement of an interval’s absolute point in time. Shifting some time interval T from point A to B implies that any time intervals previously located around B now overlap with T. Since an individual can’t perform both time intervals as specified simultaneously4, the usurped time interval must be relocated. Shifting necessitates rearrangements and rearrangements can be unpleasant. Think of this like the times some unforeseen occurrence completely ruined your plans.

  3. Insertion/Deletion: Insertion is the creation of a time interval at some point in time and deletion is the complete removal of a time interval. Since we can’t create or destroy time, the insertion of a time interval necessitates the partial or entire deletion of one or more other time intervals. Think of this as ‘freeing up space’ for the inserted interval.

  4. Transmutation: Transmutation is the modification of the nature of the time interval itself. It could mean modifying a task subsumed by the interval. It could also mean rearranging the order of the task5 or even changing the setting in which the task is completed. I shouldn’t have to explain how transmutation—by far the most complex of the four specified transformations—can behave in messy ways.

You may have observed that the messiness of these transformations follows from the non-uniformity of time. Indeed, if time was uniform, we could much more easily compare schedules.

Time Is Stubborn

You know how you might feel very picky about when you perform a task and how it’s performed? This, in essence, is stubbornness. The more ‘stubborn’ a schedule is, the more sensitive someone’s utility is to transformations of the schedule. If you’re insistent on attending your aunt’s funeral (justifiably), that means you’re not very willing to do other things during that time; it would precipitously decrease your utility. This is an example of stubbornness. Stubbornness actually simplifies time optimization problems, as it imposes constraints on one’s time.

Time Is Random

Hitherto, we’ve treated time intervals as behaving predictably. We’ve examined how the sequence and transformation of time intervals might affect one’s utility. But what happens when the properties of some time interval depend not only on the sequence of events preceding it, but the random outcomes of said events. Maybe you plan to read a book after work only if your kids don’t need any help with their homework. More generally, the time optimization problem should account for our priors—our probabilistic beliefs—about the outcomes of the events of various time intervals.

Time Has Value

As an aspiring economist, I’m obligated to preach the about the opportunity cost of time. Time invested in one task is time not allocated elsewhere, an assumption reflected in our setup of the time optimization problem.

Utility Matters, Not Time

I’d like remind us that the time optimization problem is motivated by utility maximization; the optimal schedule is fundamentally one that maximizes expected utility. Our internal notions of utility can be amorphous, arbitrary, illusory, and highly subjective. This is why an optimal schedule is indeterminable. This is why we impose constraints, employ heuristics, and simplify. Although a true solution to the time optimization problem is impossible, I hope a more philosophically thorough paradigm of time can help us obtain more accurate solutions.

In summary, in my proposed paradigm of time, we begin with the realization that time is non-uniform. The utility of an event varies by its situation: its exact point in time and the events preceding it. From this we obtain the time optimization problem, which entails simplifying the future into possible tasks represented as carefully conceived and ordered time intervals. Due to the implausibility of a truly optimal schedule, we seek a sufficiently close to optimal schedule, a problem made easier through constraints and simplifications. We see that transformations of a schedule, such as scaling, shifting, insertion/deletion, and transmutation have ramifications. It’s important to notice that time is stubborn, that outcomes are random, and that time optimization is motivated by utility maximization.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

Birth Lottery is a website that helps put this into perspective.

2

Note that these time segments need not be a singular, certain quantity. We often plan time intervals as having an estimated range of possible durations.
