For instance, I might be reasonably confident that studying for a particular quiz will take between 60 and 70 minutes. Of course, the true duration may fall outside of this interval.

3

In fact, these returns are eventually negative. It’s possible to study for so long that you’re actually accomplishing less.

4

If someone out there wants to nitpick that some thought experiment in theoretical physics allows for weird cases like this, I’m all ears. If you couldn’t tell, this article doesn’t account for pathological temporal cases, like time travel or a multiverse or immortality.

5

The difference between this and shifting is that shifting leaves the original time interval intact. It’s sort of like the difference between moving a pizza and swapping two of its slices. This also introduces a more philosophical discussion of just what constitute a time interval, as we can theoretically have time intervals nested inside of time intervals. To make this paradigm of time more accessible, I’ll refrain from delving down this rabbit hole.

item.title: Is Economics Too Ideological?
item.description: Epistemic Status: I’m a 2nd year undergraduate student majoring in econ and math.
item.content:encoded:
Epistemic Status: I’m a 2nd year undergraduate student majoring in econ and math. I have a fairly surface-level exposure to the various sub-fields of economics. I was a ‘math person’ before also becoming an ‘econ person’; I was drawn to economics because of its use of math, making me biased in favor of typical uses of math in economics. This article is opinionated, but aims to provide readers the information to argue for or against my views.

There’s a large camp of people who attack traditional economics, proposing some kind of fringe revolution in how we understand economics. These criticisms of the field of economics can be well-encapsulated as one criticism: economics is too ideological. I want to examine how three different kinds of ideology influence the field of economics1:

  1. Political ideology: How do political/economic ideologies such as Marxism and libertarianism influence economics?

  2. Institutional ideology: How do various practices in economics research and institutions, including but not limited to p-hacking, academic culture, and the publish-or-perish mentality influence economics?

  3. Economic ideology: How do more paradigmatic beliefs (e.g. using mathematical models vs. behavioral studies) influence economics?

There is admittedly some overlap between these three kinds of ideology. Much of what I discuss should be generalizable to other fields (particularly social sciences), the institution of academia, and (more ambitiously) group epistemics.

Political Ideology

A common criticism of economics is that it’s ‘too political’. Why is it that so-called ‘economists’ or pundits who purport a mastery of economics are peddling populist narratives that actually serve the global elite? At least that’s the crux of this argument. It’s important to keep in mind that experts2 in any field, when beholden to their employer, can spout propaganda. Indeed, many economists are hired to present economic arguments in service of their employer.

This is prominent in economic consulting, a profession that provides advisory services in anti-trust cases. For example, suppose the Department of Justice (DOJ) sues Meta, alleging excessive market power, among other anti-trust issues, in the realm of social media. Meta and the DOJ typically each confer with economic consultants, who can equip these two ideologically diametric parties with technical economic arguments to leverage in court. I’m simplifying here, but the DOJ might say that Meta’s market share of social media is too large, while Meta might argue that the barriers to entry are sufficiently low.

Does this mean we can’t trust economists? Not necessarily. Take my words with a grain of salt, but the average person can trust a consensus among academic economists, as opposed to private sector economists, who, in some cases, are arguably shills. The exception to this is forecasts3 and very broad political prescriptions4, as these are exceedingly difficult to make with high certainty. There are always uncertainties and errors in any field of human knowledge. The economy is too complex to be perfectly comprehended.

What about Marxism and trickle-down economics? Political ideology has historically influenced some economic theories. Milton Friedman had famously libertarian economic beliefs. John Maynard Keynes emphasized government interventionism5. Does this mean that economics isn’t a sanctuary away from political polarization? Kind of. Although economics has become increasingly empirical and consequently increasingly divorced of political ideology, it’s still present.

Most pertinently, when empirical economic methods struggle to establish a consensus, political ideology may sort people into ideological camps. In development economics, my foremost field of interest, there is a debate between two camps:

  1. Poor people don’t know what’s best for themselves. We (typically educated Westerners) should decide for them.

  2. Poor people know what’s best for themselves. We should give them the resources to make these decisions.

The ‘solution’ to this debate is truly context-dependent. There’s evidence in favor of both camps. In these kinds of cases, political ideology can sort economists into one of the two camps. This is dangerous because ‘empirical’ methods in social science come with so many caveats that they’re usually at least somewhat controvertible. The methods of studies in empirical economics are influenced by preconceived opinions to some extent. If an economist believed in the first camp, for instance, they might purposely study an economic context that they anticipate will produce evidence in favor of their beliefs. They could, in theory, only publish their results if it supports their worldview6. This hardly erodes my trust in economics because over time a preponderance of evidence can settle, or at least progress, debates influenced by political ideology.

Political ideology could also influence the research interests of economists. Maybe pro-immigration economists are more likely to study immigration. Political ideology could influence the kinds of questions asked as well. A pro-immigration economist might ask “Does immigration increase the wages of workers in the host country?” while an anti-immigration economist might ask “Does immigration increase crime in the host country?” These kinds of biases aren’t necessarily problematic and are fairly intractable. Of course people are curious about different things. Political ideology is only one contribution to this difference.

It’s also worth mentioning that economics departments in the vast majority of US universities are left-leaning. That said, an economist and a non-economist of roughly the same political leaning could have starkly different economic beliefs. This is to say that I don’t see political leaning as corrupting the exact policy stances of economists.

Institutional Ideology

Less discussed is how ideologies entrenched in the economics profession have influenced economics. Academia as a whole imposes a strong set of incentives to routinely publish statistically significant results. This encourages economists to p-hack, to knowingly or unknowingly manipulate experimental methodology to artificially inflate the statistical significance of results. I would highly recommend this paper on the practice of p-hacking and its motivations in economics.

This obsession with publishing flashy results discourages researchers from reporting statistically insignificant results (i.e. showing that some variable has no meaningful relationship with another one). This paper explains that statistically insignificant results are actually more epistemically valuable. A nontechnical way to conceptualize it is that statistically significant results affirm a prior belief, meaning you don’t exactly gain new information. Insignificant results, on the other hand, force you to update your beliefs.

The publish-or-perish quality of academia—the cutthroat incentives to publish routinely—discourage researchers from pursuing more intellectually risky topics. Indeed, how should the incentives of academia tradeoff between low-payoff, low-risk research versus high-payoff, high-risk research? There are realms of the hinterland of human knowledge unexplorable without such an ambitious, risky expedition. Despite this, I don’t entirely disagree with academia’s demand for routine publishing. For academia to allow people to explore esoteric topics, said people must have something to show for it. Furthermore, tenured faculty, researchers who have graduated from such pressures, are likely the ones most equipped to tackle riskier topics. Publish-or-perish exists for a reason.

A more valid ideological criticism is that economics overemphasizes prestige. The ranking of one’s PhD program heavily influences graduation prospects, particularly in academia. PhD admissions committees greatly value the prestige of an applicant’s recommenders. To an extent of borderline nepotism, members of admissions committees prefer applicants whose letters of recommendation come from a familiar name. Never mind the fact that some undergrads attend institutions with access to less prestigious faculty. The economics profession is no stranger to the role of prestige in society, but this doesn’t make it any better.

Economic Ideology

Part of what makes economics so simultaneously powerful and divisive is its paradigms. For instance, there’s an assumption underlying economic models that agents are rational—essentially, they make decisions that maximize their expected utility. A common refrain is that people in the real world aren’t always rational. This has been empirically shown countless times7. I have several rebuttals:

  1. Assuming rationality at least in some capacity is necessary for economic models to have value8. To see why, suppose agents in an economic model are allowed to be irrational. Then their behavior is completely unpredictable and uncircumscribed; if people don’t behave according to any patterns, then we can’t understand their decisions whatsoever.

  2. The rationality assumption can approximate real world behavior in some contexts, especially when analyzing aggregate human behavior. Some people can behave anomalously here and there, but this might be mere noise in some contexts.

  3. The rationality assumption allows us to isolate the effects of modifying incentive structures (this is basically what economists call comparative statics).

The refrain that people aren’t always rational stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of what rationality is. Rationality in the context of economics isn’t necessarily intelligence or a lack of emotion. I reiterate that rationality is people doing what makes them best off in a given situation.

Some economists have proposed neuroeconomics, which entails the use of psychological and neurological evidence in validating economic theories and in welfare analysis (see this paper for a more robust argument). I can buy that psychological and neurological evidence could help motivate economics research. I fundamentally disagree, however, that neuroeconomics should overturn traditional economic paradigms. The power of economics comes from the structured assumptions and modeling it employs. This structure is fundamentally incompatible

A broader paradigm is the extensive use of mathematics in economic modeling. And I’m not talking about the statistics used in empirical economics or the algebra used in finance. Mathematical formalism, mathematical structures, and highly theoretical setups underpin economic theory. Is this warranted? On one hand, economic theory paved the way for empirical economics. It also helps isolate economic phenomena and motivate work in empirical economics. On the other hand, it can prove radically inaccurate9. The solutions seems to be to use economic theory carefully, keeping mindful of its limitations and foreseeing its potential practical applications.

I can see another criticism of economic theory, that it diverts talented people from working on more practical problems. This criticism feels weak, because economists increasingly specialize in empirical work; the profession has demonstrably embraced the shift away from theory.

I’ve heard some argue that economists are too obsessed with quantifiability. Wealth, for instance, can’t fully capture someone’s happiness. Economics hardly concerns itself with less quantifiable aspects of society, like culture and aesthetic values. I argue that attempts to study more amorphous, subjective facets of society necessarily deviate from economic methods and are therefore the province of other fields, like sociology, anthropology, history, psychology, and philosophy. Adjacent fields can motivate and inform the way economics is done. In fact, I think good economics should acknowledge interdisciplinary perspectives. However, I am currently satisfied with the delineations between economics and adjacent fields.

Another criticism, moreso among those interested in epistemology or metascience, is that economics fails to mimic the scientific method. The properties of scientific discovery are of little interest to scientists because these properties are baked into natural science. Social scientists, on the other hand, should take caution in the use of empirical economic methods to make claims about reality. I feel the epistemic validity of empirical economic methods is well conceptualized and warrants its own article. The Two Fundamental Problems of the Theory of Knowledge by Karl Popper discusses two foundational dilemmas in asserting that an economic theory preserves relevant properties of scientific discovery:

  1. The Problem of Induction: If X phenomenon occurs 1000 times, will it necessarily occur for the 1001th time?

  2. The Problem of Demarcation: What makes a theory scientific?

The problem of induction is difficult enough to solve when proposing a theory in natural science. In social science, we have to employ a combination of educated guesswork and clever experimental design across a variety of scenarios.

The problem of demarcation is more straightforward. Suppose we have two theories to explain why day and night exist:

  1. The Earth revolves around the Sun.

  2. The Earth is inside the eye of a giant. When the giant closes its eyes, night occurs. When it opens its eyes, day occurs.

We know that both theories are false explanations of day and night. According to Popper, the first one is scientific and the second one is not. This is because the former theory is falsifiable; it can be proven wrong. I feel that falsifiability should underlie more of economic theory10.

Conclusion

Is economics too ideological? In my view, mostly no. Its most damaging ideological problems are present in most fields and exist for a reason. Many of its ‘problems’ are either not so problematic or are features of the field.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

I’m refer to ‘economics’ and ‘the field of economics’ almost interchangeably. This distinction is largely inconsequential.

2

I use the term ‘expert’ cautiously. Even experts who strive for objectivity can be wrong.

3

I’m open to persuasion that economists can become good enough at forecasting to provide worthwhile forecasts. Forecasting isn’t traditionally the focus of economics, contrary to popular belief. Therefore, a failure of economists to make worthwhile forecasts is likely due to the difficulty of making such forecasts and a lack of forecasting practice, as opposed to incompetence among economists.

4

I would argue that broader political prescriptions, if made at all, may fall outside the province of economists. Economists are more suited to answering empirical political questions, particularly those of high specificity.

5

I hesitate to label Keynesian economics as ‘political’ because it has, to my knowledge, a strong empirical basis.

6

In practice, the decision to publish results has more to do with whether the results are statistically significant than whether they affirm an economist’s ideology. This is because academia has a tendency to underreport statistically insignificant results.

7

Daniel Kahneman showed many patterns of irrationality in his work.

8

There’s this notion of revealed preferences in economics that can’t really exist without rationality. In its simplest form: if someone chooses A over B, then they must prefer A. Without rationality, these basic properties can’t hold.

9

There’s a relevant quote misattributed to Yogi Berra: “In theory there is no difference between theory and practice, while in practice there is.”

10

Empirical economics already addresses the problem of demarcation.

item.title: The Flaws of Media Ratings
item.description: Why you shouldn't rate a movie a 9 out of 10.
item.content:encoded:
Epistemic Status: This article is primarily a philosophical opinion piece. If you find my central claim very obvious, I would still encourage you to read until the end.

I’m a media anti-realist. I don’t believe that media (TV shows, films, video games, etc.) have objective quality. It probably isn’t very surprising, therefore, that I despise the 1-10 scale of rating media. Perhaps more frustrating than when people rate their own experiences with media is when people try to compare each other’s ratings. “X show was a 9 for me but a 7 for him,” I’ve heard people articulate. The flaws of this scale actually reveal many fascinating limitations of our abilities to assess subjective human experiences, such as happiness, suffering, and love. Plus, it gives me an excuse to mature people’s way of thinking about media ratings.

Ratings Are Noisy

Let’s begin by examining just how ‘noisy’ media ratings can be. First, media ratings fail to capture how our perceptions of a piece of media can change over time. What if a movie I fell asleep during as a kid could become my new favorite film if I just re-watched it? What if a book I didn’t comprehend the deeper message of as a kid seems much more enjoyable to me in retrospect?

Second, media ratings are susceptible to factors completely unrelated to the piece of media in question. What if I watched a movie while sleep deprived? What if I watched a romance film after a breakup, biasing me against romanticized portrayals of love? Or maybe watching a romance film has the opposite effect in this scenario; maybe it restores my faith in romantic relationships. Some video games are much less challenging as an adult than as a kid. And consuming a piece of media that already has sentimental value could sway one’s rating; I eagerly anticipated Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, for instance.

Individual Ratings Aren’t Comparable

Everyone has unique preferences regarding the media they consume. These preferences could shape from one’s personality, socio-cultural environment, and genetics—all of which are unique to each individual. Herein is the futility of comparing one person’s 9/10 score to another person’s 9/10 score. You may object that some individuals, in some contexts, have sufficiently comparable media preferences. If you and I both Breaking Bad, surely we both love Better Call Saul, right? As I’ll now discuss, the likelihood that two individuals have reliably comparable media preferences is, for most intents and purposes, astronomically low.

Ratings Aren’t One-Dimensional

Media ratings are an assertion of one’s perception of overall quality and/or their overall enjoyment of a piece of media. I argue that the composite of these two assertions is significantly reductive. It fails to express the more nuanced aspects of our enjoyment; poignant monologues, thought-provoking repartee, and exhilarating fights can induce distinct, yet similarly enjoyable emotions. My 9/10 and your 9/10 appraisals could be assigned for radically divergent reasons.

This begs the question: what even is ‘overall quality’ and/or ‘overall enjoyment’? I’ve already argued against the existence of objective overall quality. While I concede the existence of subjective overall quality, such as the legibility of prose in a novel, this is impossible to definitively or satisfactorily condense into a rating. It’s also unclear what overall enjoyment (which is inherently subjective) could be defined as. As aforementioned, a myriad of complex emotional experiences can constitute enjoyment. To see why this is problematic, suppose you’re watching a TV show where your favorite character is constantly disparaged by their emotionally abusive parents. Suppose you find this depiction of toxic parenting highly compelling, but it greatly upsets you at a personal level? How should this experience influence your rating of the TV show? Even if you were to neglect cases of extreme uncertainty as to how a facet of a piece of media influences your overall enjoyment, there is omnipresent uncertainty as to what overall enjoyment fundamentally is.

Ratings Are Ordinal

A 1-10 scale is partially ordinal, meaning the ordering of numbers 1-10 (or the closed interval [1, 10], if you’re mathematically minded and prefer a continuum of ratings) implies a weak ordering of pieces of media. In other words, ratings imply that some pieces of media are better, worse, or equal to other pieces of media on some account (objective quality, subjective quality, overall enjoyment, etc.). This implies several somewhat unintuitive properties:

  1. Transitivity: Suppose there are three novels: A, B, and C. If you rate A above B and B above C, then you rate A above C. This means that given any piece of media X that you assign a rating of r, any piece of media with a rating less than r is worse on some account. I find this unintuitive due to the multi-dimensionality of the enjoyment and quality of media.

  2. Equality: Any two pieces of media with the same rating are equally ‘good’ on some account. Again, the multi-dimensionality of our experiences with media complicate this. You may object that your ratings are so precise that you’ve assigned no two pieces of media the same rating. For example, you might rate Dark Souls a 9.01 and Dark Souls III a 9.01.1

  3. Completeness: All pieces of media must have some rating. If you disagree, then this implies that the rating system is only applicable to the subset of media you’ve experienced that can be assigned a rating. In such a case, you have to make a flawed, arbitrary judgement of what media to assign a rating.

  4. Monotonicity: Higher ratings are strictly better than lower ratings. This is axiomatic in the construction of a rating system.

Ratings are (Optionally) Cardinal

A 1-10 scale can optionally be cardinal, meaning we care about the exact size of numerical ratings, not just their ordering. This also suggests two even more unintuitive implications:

  1. Scale: If one book is rated a 5/10 and another is rated a 10/10, is the latter twice as ‘good’? More generally, if ratings are cardinal, we must be able to say that for any two ratings a and b, a rating of a must be x times as good as a rating of b. I reiterate that multi-dimensionality complicates this. It’s hard to say that I enjoyed some piece of media twice (or any arbitrary amount) as much as another piece of media.

  2. Arithmetic: You can do arithmetic with cardinal ratings. For example, you can say that watching a 10/10 movie is equivalent (at least on some account of enjoyment and/or quality) to watching two 5/10 movies. You can say that the difference between your enjoyment of a 10/10 movie and your enjoyment of a 3/10 movie is a 7/10 movie.

Ratings are an Aggregation

Ratings are an aggregation of our experience of consuming a piece of media. And how exactly do we perform this aggregation?

One approach is to think of ourselves as experiencing overall enjoyment on a 1-10 scale over infinitesimally small intervals of time (e.g. I feel a 9/10 exactly 5 minutes into a film). Our rating is then our average rating across these infinitesimally small intervals of time.2 This is the approach many of us like to think we can approximate when asked to rate a piece of media. I find that we can’t, in practice.

Another approach is to average our enjoyment across the intervals of time most memorable to us when consuming a piece of media. This feels closer to what we do in practice. This method is flawed because we may only remember selective parts of our experience with a piece of media. Flawed recollections can impair our retrospective views on pieces of media.

The final relevant approach is to ‘wing it’. Forget approximations of numerical methods like continuous averages or selective averages. Why not just say how you feel? This method, more than the other two, is susceptible to the peak-end rule, a phenomenon whereby subjective human experiences are largely based on the most enjoyable part of an experience and the end of the experience.

Of course, all three of the aforementioned methods of aggregation assume that we can assign ratings in the first place: a flawed assumption rocking precariously on a flimsy foundation of flawed assumptions.

Ratings are a Self-Reported Measure of Subjective Phenomena

Self-reported ratings of subjective phenomena succumb to number of other flaws3:

  1. Range: Someone who hasn’t consumed much media might assign a rating of 1/10 to their least favorite piece of media and a 10/10 to their favorite piece of media. What happens, then when they encounter two new pieces of media, which they dislike much more than the 1/10 piece of media and like much more than the 10/10 piece of media, respectively? This flawed sense of ‘range’ is also exhibited when people are asked to self-report their overall happiness, with 1 as absolute misery and 10 as pure bliss. A child might feel that scraping their knee is a 1/10 and that eating pizza is a 10/10. Then as an adult they might find that bereavement is a 1/10, scraping your knee is a 4/10, eating pizza is a 7/10, and having a child is a 10/10.

  2. Environment of Comparison: Some people’s measure of self-reported happiness is calibrated to the perceived happiness of those around them. For instance, I might rate my happiness lower if my neighbors are the happiest people on Earth (figuratively speaking). Similarly, if all your friends are exalting Stranger Things as divine nectar, you might rate it a 9/10 instead of a 7/10.

  3. Social Desirability Bias: Some people might rate a piece of media differently to seem more socially desirable. This is different from the calibration of ratings to those around you because it is purely to do with a desire for social approval.

  4. Incomparability Across Mediums: Are a 7/10 assigned to a video game and a 7/10 assigned to a music album even comparable? I reiterate—you guessed it—that multi-dimensionality complicates this.

Alternative Rating Scales

Hitherto, we’ve exclusively examined the discrete and continuous 1-10 rating scale. What if you rate all pieces of media you’ve consumed on a scale of 1-100 or from 1 to 5 stars? What if you assign pieces of media a ‘thumbs up’ or ‘thumbs down’? You can verify for yourself that virtually any rating scale succumbs to the slew of aforementioned flaws.

How to Use Ratings

If ratings are so flawed, then what uses are there for ratings?

One use of ratings is as a proxy for the probability of your enjoyment of a piece of media and/or a prior on a possible experience with a piece of media. For instance, I could analyze the IMDB rating of a TV show, the consistency in its episode ratings, the extent to which episode ratings increase over time, and the ratings my friends assigned the show.

Another use of ratings is to help establish patterns in your experiences with pieces of media. If I created a spreadsheet with a list of TV shows and the ratings I assigned each of them on the typical discrete 1-10 scale, I could implement a machine learning algorithm to identify patterns in my enjoyment of media. I might find, hypothetically, that I love mystery novels featuring an anti-hero detective. I could weigh this finding in my decision of whether to begin a piece of media.

The broader societal purposes of ratings include:

  1. To benefit reviewers

  2. To promote pieces of media

  3. As a heuristic for complex perceptual experiences

  4. As a social signal (e.g. I have ‘good’ taste so you should think I’m intelligent)

  5. To help people make an informed decision:

    1. of whether to access a piece of media

    2. of whether to pay a cost (monetary or otherwise) to access a piece of media

    3. of whether and/or under what circumstances to continue a piece of media4

Conclusion

Rating systems are a beyond flawed method of simplifying our experiences with pieces of media. I am staunchly in favor of reallocating some of the media discourse from discussions of quality to discussions of other aspects of media. To me, one of the greatest signs of media literacy is the ability to appreciate aspects of media not by assigning the label of ‘quality’, but by speaking more abstractly. At the risk of sounding pretentious: a chef describes a dish in its specific flavor, not entirely in how ‘good’ or ‘bad’ it is.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

If you believe that the probability distribution of the rating of a piece of media is continuous, then mathematically there’s zero probability that any two pieces of media have the same rating.

2

We’re essentially computing the average value of a function via integration. In this case, the limits of integration are the start and end time of the consumption of a piece of media. The independent variable is a rating in the closed interval [1, 10] and we integrate with respect to time.

3

Interestingly, many of these flaws are present in measures of self-reported happiness.

4

An example of this is when a friend tells you to continue a piece of media because it will ‘get good’.

item.title: Some Interesting Things (#1)
item.description: Learn why impossible things can happen, nothing has any probability, and nothing is a fact
item.content:encoded:
Disclaimer: I’ve had a lot of ideas that warrant sharing, but don’t warrant an entire article. This format is inspired by Noahpinion’s “At Least Five Interesting Things” articles.

Epistemic Status: This is a list of largely unrelated ideas, accordingly of varying epistemic status; some ideas are empirical facts, some are musings, etc.

1. Continuous probability is weird

Some quantities are continuous. Informally, there are no “gaps” in these quantities. An example of this is height. Someone could be 180 cm tall or 181 cm tall. But they could also be as tall as any precise quantity between 180 cm and 181 cm. In practice we round to the nearest unit of measurement, but in reality when we say that someone’s height is 180 cm, it’s actually some infinitely long string of digits (e.g. 180.234587023945…)1.

Now suppose we have a stopwatch that randomly stops at any precise time2 between 0 seconds and 1 second with uniform density. Think of this as the stopwatch being equally likely to stop at any point in that interval. What’s weird about continuous probability is that the probability that the stopwatch stopped on any singular quantity (e.g. 0.5) is exactly zero. To see why, recall that continuous quantities can be infinitely precise. That is, the stopwatch might stop on the quantity 0.500001 instead of 0.5.

An unintuitive implication of this is that when we observe the stopwatch, the quantity observed manifested with zero probability. Something with zero probability actually happened. That’s crazy to me. It fundamentally challenges the notion of zero probability as “impossibility”. It means that continuous quantities like the precise dimensions of an object/organism occur with zero probability at an instant in time.

This doesn’t really have practical implications though. Observations aren’t truly made at an “instant” in time. Our measurement instruments aren’t nearly precise enough to observe true continuity. For example, a weighing scale can’t tell the difference between 100 kg and 100.00000001 kg.3In everyday life, we can think of quantities as being “approximately continuous,” or having “small gaps”. The one practical implication I can think of is a rebuttal to the fine-tuning argument; just because the probability that our universe’s physical properties are suitable for life is zero (in the absence of God) doesn’t necessitate the impossibility of atheism. As I’ve just established, zero probability events can occur.

2. You can’t assign probabilities to everything

Sometimes people assign probabilities to events like the existence of God or the simulation hypothesis. I would argue that this isn’t logically valid because probabilities can only be assigned to events subsumed within a well-defined sample space. We can think of a sample space as the set of possible outcomes of a random occurrence. For example, if we flip a coin, the sample space contains two possibilities: heads and tails. When I say well-defined, I mean that all possibilities must unambiguously correspond to an outcome in the sample space. Moreover, these outcomes should be unambiguously defined. In the case of a coin flip, the sample space is well-defined; the coin can only land on heads or tails and there’s no ambiguity as to what “heads” or “tails” means4.

What if we try assigning probabilities to the existence of God? What is the sample space? You might be tempted to say that the sample space contains two outcomes: 1) God exists 2) God doesn’t exist. Except we can’t assign probabilities to either outcome because the sample space isn’t well-defined. We don’t have a rigorous definition of what it means for God to exist the way we have a rigorous definition of the “heads” side of a coin. Let’s refer to my stance, the necessity of a well-defined sample space when assigning probabilities, as definitionism.

Definitionism precludes the assignment of probabilities to the following questions:

  1. What is the probability that Person A becomes a bad person within the next year?

  2. What is the probability that we live in a simulation?

  3. What is the probability that the economy gets better?

It’s possible to assign probabilities to the 1st and 3rd questions with some more precise wording. For example, you could define “becomes a bad person” as “is convicted of murder” and define economic improvement as “inflation decreases 1% in the US.”

What’s interesting about the second question, however, is that I can’t think of a sensible way to define the sample space. If we live in a simulation, the reality that subsumes are simulation need not necessarily obey the same rules as ours. Much in the same way that a blind person can’t fathom color, we may be unable to fathom the properties of the “true” reality (in the event we live in a simulation). This may imply that we can’t define the sample space for us living in a simulation. It would be like asking a blind person to assign probabilities to someone’s shirt color on a given day.5

A curse of definitionism is that it’s unclear the requirements for an outcome contained within the sample space to be “unambiguous,” which brings me to the next point.

3. Nothing is a fact

I was taught in elementary school that statements can either be facts or opinions. A fact is a statement that is “true.” An opinion is a subjective expression. Facts are commonly deemed true for one of many (not all-encompassing) reasons:

  1. They are true by definition/logical consistency. For example, it is a fact that the number 3 is odd because of how humans have defined odd numbers.

  2. They are some property of the natural universe.6

  3. They are true by consensus. For example, as far as I know, Texas and Oklahoma agree on the border between them.

I believe that there are properties of the natural universe that are facts and that our “scientific facts” are our best attempts to describe these properties. But can we consider a non-scientific statement or an uncertain scientific statement a fact? Here are some examples:

  1. US GDP in 2025 was X USD. GDP is a human construction with guidelines, so in theory, GDP calculations that obey these guidelines are factual.7 However, guidelines for GDP calculation are not always unambiguous. Additionally, the data used in GDP calculations could be flawed, whether due to misreporting, measurement error, etc. The standards for GDP accounting are arguably flawed8. To what extent are official GDP numbers a fact?

  2. X latitude, longitude coordinate is a part of Y country as opposed to Z country. Political borders, in some cases, are considered a fact by consensus. Can a political border be considered a fact when it’s disputed? Probably not. But what do we consider a sufficient “dispute” for a political border to no longer be a “fact?” If I alone dispute a well-established political border, does the border cease to be a fact?

  3. Aspartame causes cancer. As of the time of writing, to my knowledge, Aspartame—a sweetener in Diet Coke—is not a known carcinogen. I imagine the way to test this is to apply statistical causal inference methods to a natural experiment or a Randomized Control Trial (RCT). Essentially, researchers could observe that the probability that aspartame causes cancer is significantly high. But then there’s some element of uncertainty. Do we need certainty to classify something as a fact?

The epistemic requirements for a “fact” are so vague that I’m not sure that any statement—barring statements that are a fact by definition—can be a fact. Maybe it’s more appropriate to view facts and opinions as a spectrum. My rule is that if a statement satisfies some subjective, ill-defined epistemic requirements, it’s a fact. Otherwise, it’s either false or an opinion.

4. Nothing can truly occur with probability 1

If I roll a standard six-sided dice, the probability that it lands on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 is 1. In other words, the probability that one of all possible outcomes occurs is 1. Big shocker. Of course an event can occur with probability 1. My claim is a more Bayesian one (don’t worry if you don’t know what Bayesianism is): the probability of an event, given my observation of an outcome, is strictly greater than zero and strictly less than one. Formally:

Informally, I can never be certain of anything. Suppose I role a standard six-sided dice and observe that it landed, unambiguously, on a 3. Ex post, the probability that the dice landed on a 3 should be 1, right?9 Well, my perception of reality is flawed. I could be hallucinating that the dice landed on a 3. Maybe I’m starving thus mentally incoherent. Maybe I’m schizophrenic.

Now you might think that this is stupid. Maybe it is. Obviously humans are prone to mistakes. Isn’t this just semantic pedanticism? Not really. If you account for the probability of incorrect observations due to human error, it can radically change the results of more complex probability problems. For example, suppose I’m playing a game where my opponent and I take turns choosing a number from 1-6 (the exact rules of the game are irrelevant here). I heard my opponent play the number 2, unambiguously. Suppose that if I play 6 in response to 2, I win. However, if I play 6 in response to any other number, I lose. This means that the probability I win the game is the probability that my opponent played 2 given that I observed him playing 2. The probability that I observed my opponent improperly might be insanely low (some ϵ > 0). Yet, if I experienced some probability of observation error on every turn, the probability that I win could be way different.10

I’m gonna call this belief about probability the uncertainty hypothesis.11 It’s not a critique of the foundations of probability so much as a belief about the way we apply/think about probability.

5. US net migration is negative

For the first time since 1935, more Americans are leaving the country than are entering.12 Should this persist, the US national debt, nearly $40 trillion as of the time of writing, could pose an unprecedented strain on the economy. Although the US doesn’t necessarily have to pay back all of its national debt by a specific deadline, larger debt results in more interest payments as a share of tax revenue. A shrinking American population would not only have less overall tax revenue, but effectively have a smaller budget per capita. The US would also have less of an ability to leverage economies of scale with a smaller population.

A smaller population could also result in diminishing US geopolitical hegemony, for better or for worse. To maintain current military spending and frontier AI research, the government would likely divert more of its budget away from social safety nets, which the current administration already deems a luxury. Perhaps we’ll see a relaxing of barriers to immigration and subsequent immigrant boom in an attempt to restore the population.

6. Can atheists believe in the simulation hypothesis?

A common reason for accepting the possibility of the simulation hypothesis (SH) is accepting that we can never outright reject its possibility; indeed, how can I confirm that I’m not living in a simulation? Similarly, a common reason for accepting the possibility of theism, the existence of God, is that we can never outright reject its possibility. The parallels between justifications for theism and the simulation hypothesis don’t end there.

Both God and a simulated reality have similar implications; there’s an individual or group of individuals in some meta-reality who created/control our reality. Both allow for the possibility of determinism, eschatology, and moral realism13. Both allow for consistency with the fine-tuning argument and Pascal's wager. In fact, you could believe in both theism and SH if you believe: 1) we live in a simulation created by God, or 2) one of God’s creations created a simulation which we live in.

My prior is that there’s a significant population of: 1) theists who fully reject SH 2) atheists who assign some credence to SH. I can’t really see a logical case for the first group, as most arguments for theism seem consistent with SH. I can, however, see a defense for the second group to employ: it’s possible to define God in such a way that anyone who could’ve created the simulation we live in isn’t God. For example, if you believe that a God would have to define moral truth and you believe that no one can define moral truth, than a creator of a simulation couldn’t be God.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1

Informally, there are more rational numbers than irrational numbers. Therefore, the probability that someone’s height at some instant in time is irrational is 1. In contrast, the probability that it’s rational is 0.

2

A clock with infinite precision is physically impossible, but this hypothetical assumes otherwise for explanatory purposes. To understand why, I highly recommend this video.

3

Furthermore, statistical methods of assessing continuous observations, such as confidence intervals, account for the fact that continuous quantities occur with zero probability.

4

If we wanted to, we could define “heads” and “tails” as fundamentally as the physical level. The “heads side” is a portion of the matter classified as a “coin” that has a particular configuration that we classify as “heads”. This may seem unnecessarily precise, but you can see how this level of thoroughness is useful in cases where it’s more difficult to define a sample space.

5

A blind person might be told that a person always wears a red shirt and form a prior accordingly, even though they can’t see color. Similarly, we can try to form inferences about a “true” reality based on proxy information, but this could be completely wrong.

6

Don’t ask me to define the “natural universe” or this is going to become too metaphysically dense. I feel like everyone has a different threshold at which they’re willing to rest on some foundational claims and stop descending an endless philosophical rabbit hole.

7

Is “true” GDP the quantity that perfectly obeys GDP accounting guidelines, or is it the quantity that these guidelines hope to approximate? It’s an interesting philosophical question.

8

Real GDP (GDP adjusted for inflation) calculates compare the price of goods/services of a previous year to those of the current year. But what happens when a good produced in the current year wasn’t previously produced? The iPhone wasn’t sold before 2007, for instance. Statistical agencies do have methods of dealing with this. My greater point, however, is that ambiguity can occur. Do such ambiguities imply that GDP numbers can’t be classified as a “fact?”

9

Accordingly, the probability that the dice landed on a 5 should be zero. If buy my argument, however, the probability that the dice landed on a 5 is nonzero (i.e. strictly positive).

10

I guess the opponent could also experience observation error, which might “cancel out.”

11

After writing this article, I discovered that this is an existing philosophical viewpoint called radical skepticism.

12

https://finance.yahoo.com/news/more-people-moving-u-moving-175548400.html

13

Some theists believe that God defines moral facts. In a simulation, you could arguably consider the morals of the creators of the simulation to be “moral facts”.

item.title: Anti-Development Economics
item.description: How to make poor countries more poor
item.content:encoded:
I realized today that the world is a good place. Too good, in fact. The solution? Increase extreme poverty worldwide. Here are some methods to accomplish this.

Method 1: Effective Charities

The Effective Altruism (EA) movement is so obsessed with creating effective charities that they’ve lost sight of what “effectiveness” actually entails. What kind of charity tries to do the most good per dollar donated? A truly effective charity would aim to achieve the most harm per dollar donated.

Some ideas for effective charities:

  • Donations to large corporations and ultrabillionaires

  • Lobby to start wars with random countries for no reason whatsoever

  • Sabotage EA global health charities

Method 2: Better Tax Policies

Lots of people say that the poor stay poor while the rich get richer. I think that’s a problem. I dream of a world where the rich get richer and the poor get poorer. Starting now, world powers should form a multilateral agreement to expropriate all the possessions of anyone outside the top income percentile.

Method 3: Corrupt Institutions

Institutions like judicial courts and democracies perversely prioritize justice over corruption. This is egregious. We need to replace the judges of judicial courts in poor countries with convicted felons. Priority should be given to felons with criminal records of the highest aggregate quantity and severity. We should also abandon traditional voting systems like first-past-the-post in favor of randomized voting. This superior voting mechanism randomly selects candidates for office, with extra probability assigned to the candidates with the least ballots.

Conclusion

I hope the field of development economics can finally wake up to see that we need to make people in developing countries more poor—not less.

item.title: Applied Population Ethics
item.description: How to envision an ideal world and chart the path to attaining it
item.content:encoded:
Epistemic status: I’m not a professional philosopher, though I’ve had my fair share of exposure to the field of population ethics. I’m going to omit some more technical assumptions and specifications for the sake of brevity and comprehension. If want to dive deeper into population ethics, I recommend reading this article, then reading this one. I discuss the assumptions I make and my personal views of population ethics here. Some of what I write is an existing part of the field, while other parts of what I write are concepts I devised myself.

This article, for simplicity, comes nowhere close to explaining every theory of population ethics or every objection to average/total utilitarianism. I also omit formal definitions for simplicity, though I’ll create a technical appendix with these definitions if enough people ask me. I assume a basic understanding of arithmetic and probability (particularly expected value calculations). Single-variable calculus is helpful and real analysis allows you to devise formal definitions for the concepts presented.

Introduction

Is it moral to give birth to a disabled child ex ante? How much near-term prosperity should society sacrifice for the long-term future? Is it ethical to kill animals? How good is a society where the happiness of many is at the expense of a few? These are just some of the questions that the philosophical field of population ethics equips us to answer.

Let’s establish some preliminaries. Suppose that the global population at an instant in time is a collection of individuals who each have some level of welfare. Welfare quantifies the overall quality of the individual’s entire life—both lived and not yet lived. We’ll treat welfare as a changing quantity later on, but let’s focus on this definition for now. An individual with positive welfare can be thought of as having a life worth living—of net happiness. In contrast, one with negative welfare can be thought of as a having a life not worth living—of net suffering. There can also exist individuals with zero welfare, which can be thought of as a net neutral life. For example, we could have a population at some instant in time with three individuals—A, B, and C—who have welfare 5, -10, and 0, respectively.

You might think it’s silly to reduce the quality of an individual’s life to a single number. Indeed, what good is a quantity that is nebulous, immaterial, reductive, and inconsistent between individuals? And who are we to decide that a person’s life isn’t worth living? There are two points to consider. First, welfare enables us to isolate the crux of population ethics before concerning ourselves with more practical considerations; it’s like ignoring the air resistance in a physics problem. Second, the exact values of welfare are irrelevant; what matters is the numerical relationships between welfare values.

More concretely, higher welfare is better than lower welfare; a person with a welfare of 10 is better off than a person with a welfare of 5. It’s important not to become deluded by exact quantities. Think of the welfare difference between a 5 and a 10 as identical1 to that between a 10 and a 15.2 It’s also important to note that I use the word “individuals” rather than “people” to refer to units of the population. This is because non-human entities, such as animals, AI agents, and aliens (hypothetically speaking), can be assigned moral patienthood (i.e. we can care about them morally). Finally, we’re going to assume that welfare values already reflect relevant practical considerations. For example, you might think that if a population consists of people of welfare -10 and 10, respectively, the happy person makes the “unhappy” person better off, subsequently increasing their welfare. Let’s assume that in these kinds of cases, the welfare values already reflect these kinds of effects. That is, the -10 already factors in the influence of the happy person. If this doesn’t make sense yet, don’t worry.

We can visualize a populations at an instant in time with a simple diagram:

Figure 1 displays the welfare distribution for populations A and B. The width of a box represents the number of individuals within that segment of the population. The height of a box represents the welfare of individuals within said segment of the population. Each box rests against a thin line—a horizontal axis—representing a welfare of 0. The number labeling the side of a box vertically away from the line indicates welfare, while the number labeling the side of a box that touches the horizontal axis represents the number of people. In Figure 1, A has 20 individuals of welfare 100 and 40 individuals of welfare 50. B has 20 individuals of welfare 0 and 40 individuals of welfare -20. Get comfortable with these diagrams.

Now we arrive at the crux of population ethics: is A better than B? Intuitively, yes. Unequivocally. Everyone in B is worse off than even the worst off members of A.3 But what if this weren’t the case? We need a more specific and therefore generalizable theory of population ethics. For the purposes of this article, I’ll limit our analyses to the two primary theories of population ethics.

Total utilitarianism is the view that populations should be compared via the sum total of their welfare. In Figure 1, A would have a total of 20 x 100 + 40 x 50 = 4000 and B would have a total of 20 x 0 + 40 x -20 = -800. I just summed the welfare of the individuals in each population. Since 4000 is greater than -800, we can say that A is better than B. Hereafter, anytime I claim that some population is “better” than another, I mean that it’s better under the theory of population ethics at hand (e.g. total utilitarianism). Similarly, worse populations are worse under a given theory of population ethics.

Average utilitarianism is the view that populations should be compared via their average (arithmetic mean4) welfare. In Figure 1, A has an average of (20 x 100 + 40 x 50)/(20 + 40) ≈ 66.67. B has an average of (20 x 0 + 40 x -20)/(20 + 40) ≈ 13.33. Average utilitarianism would assert that A is better than B because it has a higher average welfare.

Both views have their flaws. Total utilitarianism believes that adding someone to the population of positive welfare always makes the population better. This results in what’s known as the repugnant conclusion, the conclusion that a large population of individuals whose lives are barely worth living (i.e. low positive welfare) is better than a small population of individuals of high welfare.

You can verify for yourself that, in Figure 2, B is better than A according to total utilitarianism. That’s wildly unintuitive to many.5 Why should population size inherently6 make a population better?

Average utilitarianism suffers from what I’ll call the anti-egalitarian conclusion.

In Figure 3, A is better than B according to average utilitarianism (verify this yourself). This also feels unintuitive. Is a population truly better if the welfare of some is at the expense of others? Perhaps in some extremes. Suppose you do entertain the anti-egalitarian conclusion. You’re in luck, because there’s another scenario that impugns average utilitarianism. I dub this the genocidal conclusion.

In Figure 4, A’ is simply A without the 10 suffering individuals (individuals of negative welfare). Expunging the suffering people raises the average, making A’ better than A according the average utilitarianism. The genocidal conclusion implies that if suffering individuals are erased from society in a vacuum—that is, in a manner that doesn’t influence surviving individuals—society is improved. It would be like if a small, unknown tribe of suffering people were wiped from the planet.

It turns out that population ethics is a difficult problem to tackle, especially if you’re a moral realist or have “traditional” moral intuitions. Although there are many more theories of population ethics beyond average and total utilitarianism, all of these theories seem to break under some scenario. Indeed, any “prevailing” theory of population ethics must bite some kind of bullet, accepting some or the other conclusion.

I invite you to play around with your own scenarios to get accustomed to the complexity of population ethics before continuing.

Transformations

Hitherto, we’ve discussed populations at “instants” in time. We can explore the applications of population ethics more extensively if we treat populations as dynamically changing.

A population transformation is a change in a population. It includes the birth, death, and/or welfare changes of individuals. For example, in Figure 4, A’ is a transformation of A where 10 individuals of welfare -2 are killed.

Suppose A’ is a transformation of A where 2 individuals of welfare 5 are born and 5 individuals of welfare 8 have their welfare lowered to 4. This is visualized in Figure 5. You may have noticed that the box diagrams are ambiguous in conveying the order of steps in a transformation. For instance, in Figure 5, it’s possible that the following transformation occurred instead:

  • 2 of the individuals of welfare 8 had their welfare lowered to 5

  • 3 individuals of welfare 8 had their welfare lowered to 4

  • 2 new individuals of welfare 4 were born

You can verify for yourself that both transformations produce identical box diagrams. This begs a critical question: given that both transformations produce identical box diagrams (i.e. identical welfare distributions), do both transformations produce identical populations? I argue yes and will maintain this assumption from now on to circumvent any ambiguity in the box diagrams. If this seems ludicrous to you, I should specify that these transformations are instantaneous (for now at least). In the real world, changes to the population have lasting welfare impacts. The two transformations can be considered identical because any intermediate changes involved in the transformations happen instantaneously and are therefore inconsequential.7 You might think that this is silly because changes in the real world don’t occur instantaneously. Bear with me for now.

What if transformations were random? A stochastic transformation is a type of transformation where outcomes are random.

Figure 6 displays a stochastic transformation where two outcomes each occur with 50% probability:

  1. Outcome A’: The welfare of the individuals of A decreases from 6 to 4

  2. Outcome A*: The welfare of the individuals of A increases from 6 to 8. 2 individuals of welfare 8 are born. 5 individuals of welfare 4 are born.

We’ll soon have to make comparisons between various transformations and stochastic transformations.8 The simplest method of evaluating stochastic transformations is to make expected value calculations9 using a theory of population ethics. For example, under the total utilitarianism, the stochastic transformation in Figure 6 increases the value of the population from 60 to 70; the expected total welfare of the transformed population is .50 x (10 x 4) + .50 x (10 x 8 + 5 x 4) = 70. Similarly, under average utilitarianism, the stochastic transformation decreases the value of the population from 6 to approximately 5.3 (verify this yourself).

Timelines

Now we’re ready to explore how populations evolve over time. Suppose for simplicity that time is divided into years.10 We begin in year 0. A timeline of a population is a sequence of states of the population starting from year 0. Let’s begin with a simple example where we can choose between two transformations—Policy A and Policy B—applied to a population in year 0 and year 1. Policy A, increases the welfare of the same 10 individuals by 1 every year (see Figure 7A).

Policy B, adds 5 new individuals of welfare 2 to the population every year (see Figure 7B).

How do we decide which policy we prefer under a given theory of population ethics? More generally, how can we apply existing theories of population ethics across spans of time?

One approach is to take the average of the value of the population across all three years. Under total utilitarianism, the population is valued at 90, 100, and 110, respectively across the three years under both Policy A and Policy B. The average of this value is 100 with Policy A; (90 + 100 + 110)/3 = 100. Under average utilitarianism, we similarly compute the average value of the population under both policies across all three years. This average is 5 with Policy A and approximately 4.06 with Policy B. Let’s call this approach meta-average utilitarianism. Note that this is not interchangeable with average utilitarianism. Meta-average utilitarianism averages the value of the population across time. In contrast, average utilitarianism averages welfare across individuals within an instant in time. As I’ve shown, it’s possible to employ either total or average utilitarianism alongside meta-average utilitarianism.

Meta-average utilitarianism experiences its own version of the genocidal conclusion which I’ll call the decadent conclusion. The decadent conclusion is the notion that, if society is perpetually below its average across prior years (given a theory of population ethics) it would be better if that society ceased to exist.

Figure 8 illustrates a scenario where the population begins with 100 long-living aliens of welfare 20. The population remains this way for 1000 years. Beginning on year 1000, the alien’s have their welfare permanently reduced to 1. The aliens finally go extinct after year 100,000.11 Meta-average utilitarianism suggests that if the population went extinct, the years after 999 wouldn’t “drag down” the meta-average (the average value of the population across all its years). The decadent conclusion is somewhat peculiar because it contradicts our intuition that society should continue to exist as long as it’s net happy—at least as long as there’s hope that it will become net happy.

Meta-average utilitarianism also experiences something akin to the anti-egalitarian conclusion. The inconsistent conclusion is the notion that it’s acceptable for the population to experience net suffering for some years as long as the other years are good enough.

Figure 9 illustrates a scenario where, beginning in year 1, each of the 100 individuals of the population experience -1/(n+1)! welfare, where n is the year. Let’s assume again that the population goes extinct in year 100,000. Employing some mathematical wizardry12, the average value of the population across an infinite number of years is net positive under both total and average utilitarianism. It feels ridiculous to think that the prosperity of a single year is meant to outweigh virtually endless years of suffering.

Another approach is to total the value of the populations across time given a theory of population ethics. Let’s call this meta-total utilitarianism. Let’s return to the policy example illustrated in Figure 7A and Figure 7B. Under total utilitarianism, the total is 300 with both Policy A and Policy B; 90 + 100 + 110 = 300. Under average utilitarianism, the total is 15 with Policy A and approximately 12.17 with Policy B.

Meta-total utilitarianism also suffers from the inconsistent conclusion. If we apply it to the scenario illustrated in Figure 9, we find that, under both total and average utilitarianism, the value of the population is net positive. The prosperity of a single year continues to outweigh a near-eternity of suffering.

We can see that meta-total utilitarianism can also suffer from the repugnant conclusion. Imagine two timelines for a population of 10 individuals of welfare 8 (I trust that I don’t need to illustrate this diagrammatically):

  1. Every year, each individual’s welfare increases by 1.

  2. Every year, a new individual of welfare 2 is added to the population.

The second timeline is preferred under meta-total utilitarianism and total utilitarianism. This implies that it’s better to keep adding new people of lower welfare than to marginally improve the lives of existing people. In contrast, the first timeline is preferred under meta-total utilitarianism and average utilitarianism. Both may feel unintuitive in their own ways. Pick your poison.

We limit our discussion of methods for evaluating populations across time to meta-average and meta-total utilitarianism, but feel free to devise your own theories. For simplicity, I’ve neglected to supply an example for either method that involves stochastic transformations (note that it’s fairly straightforward).13

Discounting and Moral Patienthood

Hitherto, our calculations involving meta-total and meta-average utilitarianism have treated each year as equally important. The standard practice of economics, finance, and parts of philosophy is instead to discount future years. In the case of discrete time14 (e.g. when the years go 0, 1, 2, and so on), we can multiply the value each year (given a theory of population ethics) by some discount factor β raised to the power of said year. For example, the value of year 2 is multiplied by β squared. Here are some of the reasons we use discount factors to value the future less heavily:

  • The future is rife with uncertainty. For example, I’m much more likely to die 50 years from now than 10 years from now.

  • People tend to have a present bias (i.e. we want rewards now).

  • There are opportunity costs to decisions made in the present. For example, instead of spending $30,000 a year to attend college, I could invest that money into an index fund.

Another worthwhile addition to our theories is adjustments for moral patienthood. One approach is to apply a monotonic transformation. Don’t worry if the proceeding explanation doesn’t make sense to you (this concept honestly warrants an article of its own). This entails applying a different monotonic function to each category of moral patient. For example, suppose you have a population of 10 humans of welfare 8 and 10 cows of welfare 6. Let’s arbitrarily choose a function to apply to cows: f(x) = .5x, where x is any welfare value. In other words, the welfare of a cow is weighted as half that of a human. Thus, under total utilitarianism, the value of this population is 10 x 8 + 10 x (.5 x 6) = 110.

Applications

We now have the prerequisites to apply population ethics to the real world.

I’ve found population ethics especially useful for thinking about animal welfare. First, is it ethical to kill wild animals? For simplicity, let’s assume that all wild animals have equal moral patienthood, all wild animals are identical, wild animal deaths are independent (i.e. one wild animal death doesn’t cause another one), and wild animal welfare doesn’t influence human welfare. Figure 10 illustrates a scenario where a local businessperson in a town wants to destroy swampland to construct a new mall.

As you can see above, the construction of the mall makes the population worse off according to total utilitarianism and better off according to average utilitarianism.

The simplicity of the model allows us to isolate the moral impact of the death of a portion of the swamp fauna. This ability to “isolate” moral quandaries is what makes population ethics so powerful. The beauty of this approach is that if you disagree with my modeling assumptions, you can simply re-calibrate the assumptions and still apply the same theories of population ethics. For example, you might disagree that wild animals have positive welfare. If so, simply evaluate Figure 11.

You might still disagree with the exact welfare values I chose or the specification of the transformation (e.g. the construction of the mall increases the welfare of the town’s human residents by the same amount). If so, you can play around with these assumptions using your own box diagrams.

Second, is it ethical to eat meat? More specifically, is it moral to purchase meat produced via factory-farming? Let’s make the following assumptions:

  • My marginal purchase of meat leads to the subsequent breeding of more animals in a factory farm in expectation.15 That is, if I purchase meat, more animals will live a life of suffering and die on average.

  • Eating meat makes me better off and that there’s a 5% chance my marginal purchase leads to the breeding of 5 more animals in factory farms. That is, the purchase is a stochastic transformation of the population.

  • Evaluate stochastic transformations using expected value

  • Humans and animals have equal moral patienthood

Given our assumptions, my purchase makes the population worse off under both total utilitarianism and average utilitarianism; 1 x 8 + 100 x -10 > .95 x (1 x 8 + 100 x -10) + .05 x (1 x 9 + 105 x -10). A very reasonable criticism of this scenario is my modeling assumption that humans and animals are equal moral patients (i.e. their welfare values are weighted equally). An easy way to account for this is to weight the animals less heavily than humans, such as by halving their welfare (recall the “Discounting and Moral Patienthood” section).

Should you have a child? Though I wouldn’t recommend solely basing this decision on your population ethical beliefs, it’s fun to think about anyways.

Assumptions:

  • I’m already happy

  • There are no externalities to having a child (i.e. this decision can’t affect the welfare of anyone besides my child or me).

  • Let’s assume for simplicity that if I choose to have a child, there are only three possible outcomes:

    • Bad Outcome: My child and I have a life of net suffering.

    • Neutral Outcome: My life is slightly worse and my child’s life is net neutral.

    • Good Outcome: My child lives a wonderful life and my life improves.

  • Evaluate stochastic transformations using expected value

As you can see in Figure 13, the population is better off according to the total view and worse off according to the average view. This model is too simplistic to be useful. First, the outcomes that arise from having a child are a continuum, not three possible outcomes. Second, it’s difficult to form priors on possible outcomes. Finally, children can be a positive externality; they can eventually benefit people other than their parents, such as by working or performing altruistic deeds. Nevertheless, population ethics helps those contemplating parenthood evaluate two far more practical questions:

  1. Should I have a kid if I know that the kid will be happy and that my happiness will become slightly lower?

  2. Should I have a kid if the kid will be less happy than most people, yet still live a net happy life?

You can see for yourself that average and total utilitarianism may yield conflicting answers to these questions.

Does the looming decline in the global human population make the world worse off? In the real world, larger populations confer a host of benefits that raise welfare almost universally: economies of scale, clustering, the transmission of knowledge, and network effects. Let’s ignore these benefits for now to examine the question exclusively from a population ethical standpoint.16 Let’s also assume that humans are the only moral patients and that all humans have the same welfare.

Without drawing box diagrams, we can see that a population decline makes the population worse according to total utilitarianism and neither better nor worse according to average utilitarianism (the average doesn’t change).

How much near-term happiness should society sacrifice for the long-term future? Suppose we have supreme control over the trajectory of AI development. If we accelerate AI development, we reap the benefits of AGI (think of it as highly advanced AI) sooner, but there’s a risk of doom (extinction or extreme suffering due to AI). If we pause AI development for a few years, we reap the same benefits later with much less risk of doom.

Assumptions:

  • Humans are the only moral patients

  • Humans have equal welfare

  • The human population remains constant

  • AI affects all humans equally

  • Once AGI is achieved, AI ceases to advance and humans cannot be made any better or worse off.

  • Stochastic transformations are evaluated using expected value

Figure 14A displays this scenario, assuming the probability of doom (P(Doom)) is 20%. For clarity, the population maintains in state in year 0 until year 10 and in year 10 until year 20. Both year 20 scenarios in the diagram persist through year 1000. Whether doom occurs is determined in year 20. That means that with 20% probability, beginning in year 20, humanity experiences net suffering for an eternity. In these figures, welfare remains the same until a change. For example, above, humanity remains at welfare 5 until year 10.

Figure 14B displays the scenario where AI progress is paused for a decade, assuming P(Doom) in this case is 5%. However, it takes an additional decade to develop AGI.

Assume a discount factor of β = 0.95. That means that the “weighting” of year 1 is .95 times that of year 0. The weighting of year 2 is (.95)^2 of year 0. Year 3 is (.95)^3 of year 0 and so on (it’s okay if this doesn’t make sense). I’m not going to show the mathematical steps17 involved in comparing AI acceleration to an AI pause (sorry, I’m lazy). Here are the results under every possible combination of average/total utilitarianism and meta-average/meta-total utilitarianism:

  • Average + meta-average: Both are equivalent (for weird mathematical reasons).18

  • Average + meta-total: Pausing is better than acceleration. Acceleration and pause both make the population better.

  • Total + meta-average: Both are equivalent (for weird mathematical reasons).

  • Total + meta-total: Pausing is better than acceleration. Acceleration and pause both make the population better.

I admittedly made quite a few simplifying assumptions and did some hand-waving here. Nevertheless, I hope you can see the bigger picture: population ethics helps us evaluate whether long-term benefits warrant near-term costs.

By now you should be familiar with the following process for modeling moral decisions using population ethics:

  1. What does the initial population look like? How many individuals are there? How much welfare do they each have?

  2. What’s the time horizon? Across how many years are we performing an evaluation? It could be zero years. Is the time horizon discrete or continuous (this is more of a mathematical consideration)?

  3. What are the transformations? Who is born/dies? How do individual welfare values change? Are any of these transformations stochastic?

  4. How do evaluate stochastic transformations? The expected value approach is the default.

  5. How do we assign moral patienthood? An easy, albeit sometimes over-simplistic, approach is to assign all individuals either full moral patienthood or no moral patienthood (as we’ve done for most of the article).

  6. How do we discount the future? The standard approach (in discrete time) is to multiply by a discount factor (as we’ve done).

  7. Which theory of population ethics do we use for evaluating each moment in time? Average and total utilitarianism are the quintessential choices.

  8. Which theory do we use to aggregate the value of a population across moments in time? In this article, we’ve used meta-average and meta-total utilitarianism.

I want to conclude our exploration of population ethics with what to me is the most profound question it could answer: What is utopia?

What is the ideal population? If you could endlessly apply any kind of transformation to a population, which transformations should you choose? The former questions asks us what the perfect population ethical world is, while the latter asks us how to attain it.

Total utilitarianism implies that a utopia is a population with infinitely positive total welfare. It implies that the composition of the population—the level of equality and the number of those suffering—is irrelevant in the grand scheme of things. The attainment of the total utilitarian’s utopia entails the eternal birth of overwhelmingly positive individuals and/or the eternal overwhelmingly positive change in the welfare of those who already exist. However, infinities behave weirdly. Observe that I use the term “overwhelmingly positive.” This is because, under total utilitarianism, we can “cancel” out deaths, births of individuals of negative welfare, and reductions in the welfare of existing individuals. For example, we could indefinitely, simultaneously birth individuals of welfare 10 and individuals of welfare -5. The total utilitarian’s utopia is perhaps not so perfect.

Average utilitarianism implies that a utopia is a population with infinitely positive average welfare. It also implies that the composition of the population is irrelevant in the grand scheme of things; the average is all that matters. The attainment of the average utilitarian’s utopia entails the eternal birth (overwhelmingly) of individuals above the current average welfare and/or eternal increases in the welfare of existing individuals. The births of those who are happy, yet not as happy as the average, are undesirable. The births of these individuals, along with those of negative welfare, can become outweighed by the births of very happy people. Or by increases in welfare in the “elites” who enjoy lives far above the average. Or by the deaths of those who live below average lives. So too can suffering persist in the average utilitarian’s utopia.

The pursuit of a population ethical utopia epitomizes some or the other unpleasant conclusion. It’s ominous, really. That we may never understand on a fundamental philosophical level what kind of world we ought to pursue.19

Objections

There are numerous flaws with applying population ethical paradigms to moral quandaries.

First, population ethics assumes that we can assign a welfare value to individuals. There’s an extensive, multidisciplinary literature that challenges traditional conceptions of utility and happiness.20 While I argue that the quantification of overall life quality enables us to make very practical moral arguments, we should exercise caution.

Second, population ethics assumes that welfare values are comparable across individuals, including humans, animals, fictional entities, aliens, and AI agents. Although I’m no expert, I’ve encountered yet another extensive, multidisciplinary literature that challenges this. Animals have a different gamut of conscious experiences from us. Moreover, some economists have argued that interpersonal welfare comparisons are meaningless.

Third, the validity of population timelines across infinite time horizons is debatable. The arguments here are mathematical. For one, how can we compare population timelines whose meta-average or meta-total utility diverges across an infinite time horizon?21 Let’s call this the infinite welfare problem. Potential resolutions to this problem are outside the scope of this article. Also, infinite time horizons should arguably account for existential risks, such as human extinction. Assigning priors to these risks is a subject of sophisticated debate.

Finally, population ethics is meaningless if you don’t believe in any form of utilitarianism. Comparing population outcomes with other moral frameworks seems to be outside the scope of the field.

Conclusion

Despite its shortcomings, population ethics has given me indispensable frameworks for conceptualizing morality. It has informed my beliefs on animal welfare and my priors on cause prioritization, among other things.

A few paragraphs ago, I left you with a very nihilistic verdict regarding population ethics. But that’s not the feeling I want to leave you with. Conviction against inequity. Compassion for the suffering. Altruism. Moral ambition. These are feelings that validate the study of population ethics.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe to support my work and receive new posts.

Our minds tend to assign diminishing magnitude to numbers. We might psychologically perceive the difference between a million and a billion as comparable to that between a billion and a trillion, for instance.
